fuentes/faragher-great-and-noble-scheme/.texto: A Great and Noble Scheme: The Tragic Story of the Expulsion of the Acadians from Their American Homeland

History of the Acadians from the British conquest of Acadia in 1710 to their deportation in 1755 and their later dispersal. It studies the decision of Governor Charles Lawrence and the Nova Scotia Council, the operations of the New England troops and the fate of the deportees.
It is the most complete history of the deportation; it argues that it was ethnic cleansing.

fuentes/diarios-de-winslow-1755/titulo.texto: Journals of Colonel John Winslow on the Siege of Beauséjour and the Deportation of the Acadians

fuentes/diarios-de-winslow-1755/resumen.texto: Journals of the commander of the New England troops at the siege of Fort Beauséjour in June 1755 and at the deportation of the Acadians from Grand-Pré in the autumn of that year. They include the speech with which Winslow gathered the men in the church on 5 September. They were published in the Collections of the Nova Scotia Historical Society in 1883 and 1884.

fuentes/diarios-de-winslow-1755/por_que_.texto: They are the account of the man who directed the deportation at Grand-Pré.

fuentes/knox-historical-journal/titulo.texto: An Historical Journal of the Campaigns in North America for the Years 1757, 1758, 1759, and 1760

fuentes/knox-historical-journal/resumen.texto: Journal of a captain of the 43rd Regiment of Foot who served as garrison in Nova Scotia (1757–1759), took part in the siege of Quebec in 1759, spent the winter of 1759–1760 in the city, and was present at Sainte-Foy and the surrender of Montreal. It includes official documents, orders and letters.

fuentes/knox-historical-journal/por_que_.texto: It is one of the most used British eyewitness sources on the Quebec campaign of 1759–1760; on Louisbourg (1758) it gathers other people's accounts.

fuentes/fowler-empires-at-war/titulo.texto: Empires at War: The French and Indian War and the Struggle for North America, 1754-1763

fuentes/fowler-empires-at-war/resumen.texto: History of the French and Indian War, from the Ohio Valley to the Treaty of Paris of 1763, with the campaigns of Louisbourg, Quebec, and Montreal and the war's final episode in Newfoundland in 1762, when the French took St. John's and the British retook it at Signal Hill.

fuentes/fowler-empires-at-war/por_que_im.texto: It is a recent synthesis of the war that covers the last battle of the Seven Years' War in North America.

fuentes/corkran-cherokee-frontier/titulo.texto: The Cherokee Frontier: Conflict and Survival, 1740-1762

fuentes/corkran-cherokee-frontier/resume.texto: History of Cherokee relations with South Carolina and Virginia up to the Anglo-Cherokee War of 1758-1761, covering trade, alliances, and clashes on the frontier. It recounts the siege of Fort Loudoun and the campaigns of Montgomery and Grant.

fuentes/corkran-cherokee-frontier/por_qu.texto: It is the classic study of the Anglo-Cherokee War.

fuentes/short-narrative-masacre-de-bosto.texto: A Short Narrative of the Horrid Massacre in Boston
Committee of the Town of Boston

Report published in Boston in April 1770 by a town committee, with sworn statements from more than ninety witnesses about the clash of March 5, the deaths of five colonists, and the role of the soldiers of the 29th Regiment. It is the patriots' version, which Captain Preston and the soldiers answered at their trial.
It fixed the name “massacre” and the patriots' version, which spread throughout the colonies.

fuentes/zobel-boston-massacre/resumen.texto: Study of the events of March 5, 1770, covering the military occupation of Boston from 1768, tensions with workers, the King Street scene, and the trials of Preston and of the soldiers, whom John Adams defended. It concludes that the soldiers were provoked and that part of the patriots manipulated the account.

fuentes/zobel-boston-massacre/por_que_im.texto: It is the reference study of the massacre and its trials, written by a lawyer and legal historian.

fuentes/frothingham-siege-of-boston/titu.texto: History of the Siege of Boston, and of the Battles of Lexington, Concord, and Bunker Hill

fuentes/frothingham-siege-of-boston/resu.texto: History of the siege of Boston from the Intolerable Acts to the British evacuation of March 1776, with the events of April 1775 and Bunker Hill. It gathers the testimony of militiamen, Gage's reports, and accounts by British soldiers.

fuentes/frothingham-siege-of-boston/por_.texto: It is the classic history of the start of the War of Independence in Massachusetts.

fuentes/fischer-paul-reveres-ride/resume.texto: It reconstructs Boston politics in 1774-1775, the work of the committees of safety, and the events of April 18 and 19, 1775, including the rides of Revere and Dawes, Lexington, Concord, and the British withdrawal. It relies on testimony from both sides.

fuentes/fischer-paul-reveres-ride/por_qu.texto: It is the leading modern account of the fighting at Lexington and Concord.

fuentes/smith-fourteenth-colony/titulo.texto: Our Struggle for the Fourteenth Colony: Canada and the American Revolution

fuentes/smith-fourteenth-colony/resumen.texto: Two-volume history of the Continental Army's invasion of Canada in 1775-1776, with the taking of Montreal, Arnold's march through Maine, the assault on Quebec on December 31, 1775, and the retreat of 1776. It uses archival documents from both sides.

fuentes/smith-fourteenth-colony/por_que_.texto: It is the classic study of the 1775-1776 Canada campaign.

fuentes/calloway-revolution-in-indian-co.texto: The American Revolution in Indian Country

It studies how the War of Independence affected the Indigenous peoples of eastern North America, including the divisions among the Iroquois, Sullivan's campaign, the war in Ohio and Kentucky, the Gnadenhutten massacre, and the battles of Oriskany, Wyoming, and Blue Licks. It shows that Indigenous peoples acted according to their own interests.
It is the standard work on the role of Indigenous peoples in the War of Independence.

fuentes/fischer-washingtons-crossing/res.texto: It narrates the New York and New Jersey campaign of 1776-1777: the defeat on Long Island, the retreat, the crossing of the Delaware, the victory at Trenton, and the one at Princeton, looking at both armies and at the Hessian mercenaries. It won the Pulitzer Prize for History in 2005.

fuentes/fischer-washingtons-crossing/por.texto: It is the modern study of the 1776-1777 campaign, centered on Long Island and Trenton.

fuentes/burgoyne-state-of-expedition/tit.texto: State of the Expedition from Canada, as Laid Before the House of Commons

fuentes/burgoyne-state-of-expedition/res.texto: The British general's defense of his 1777 campaign from Canada down the Hudson, up to his surrender at Saratoga. It includes the orders he had received, his correspondence with Howe, and the testimony of officers. He published it for the House of Commons inquiry.

fuentes/burgoyne-state-of-expedition/por.texto: It is the account of the commander defeated at Saratoga, with documents from the campaign.

fuentes/ketchum-saratoga/titulo.texto: Saratoga: Turning Point of America's Revolutionary War

fuentes/ketchum-saratoga/resumen.texto: History of Burgoyne's 1777 campaign, with the battles of Freeman's Farm on September 19 and Bemis Heights on October 7, the surrender on October 17, and its consequences, among them France's alliance with the United States.

fuentes/ketchum-saratoga/por_que_importa.texto: It is a modern monograph on the Saratoga campaign.

fuentes/graymont-iroquois-in-the-revolut.texto: The Iroquois in the American Revolution

Study of the Iroquois Confederacy in the War of Independence, from the end of its neutrality in 1777 and Oriskany, through Joseph Brant's war, the Wyoming Valley and Cherry Valley in 1778, to Sullivan's campaign of 1779. It treats the war from Iroquois and American documents.
It is the classic history of the Iroquois in the war.

fuentes/glatthaar-forgotten-allies/titul.texto: Forgotten Allies: The Oneida Indians and the American Revolution

fuentes/glatthaar-forgotten-allies/autor.texto: Joseph T. Glatthaar and James Kirby Martin

fuentes/glatthaar-forgotten-allies/resum.texto: History of the Oneidas, who allied with the patriots, and of the division of the Iroquois Confederacy. It covers their role at Oriskany and at Saratoga, their part in defending the frontier, and the loss of lands they suffered afterward.

fuentes/glatthaar-forgotten-allies/por_q.texto: It shows the Oneidas' side of the battle of Oriskany.

fuentes/diarios-de-la-expedicion-de-sull.texto: Journals of the Military Expedition of Major General John Sullivan against the Six Nations in 1779

Collection of journals kept by officers and soldiers on Sullivan's campaign, with Washington's orders, Sullivan's reports, and accounts of the destruction of Seneca and Cayuga villages and crops. The journals date from 1779 and were written in the field; New York State gathered and published them in Auburn in 1887.
They are the testimony of those who took part in the 1779 campaign.

fuentes/forbes-warriors-of-the-colorado/.texto: Warriors of the Colorado: The Yumas of the Quechan Nation and Their Neighbors

History of the Quechan (Yuma) people of the Colorado River crossing, from their encounter with the Spanish to the nineteenth century, covering the Palma alliances, the missions of 1780, and their destruction in the revolt of July 1781, in which Francisco Garcés and other friars and soldiers died.
It is the standard study of Quechan history and of their 1781 revolt.

fuentes/galvez-diario-de-pensacola/titul.texto: Diary of the Operations of the Expedition against the Stronghold of Pensacola

fuentes/galvez-diario-de-pensacola/resum.texto: Official diary of Bernardo de Gálvez's campaign against Pensacola, from March to May 1781, covering the landing, the siege, the explosion of the powder magazine of the Queen's Redoubt, and the surrender of General John Campbell. It was printed in 1781 without a place or printer, in editions attributed to Havana, Madrid, and Mexico City, and was published in the Gazeta de Madrid.

fuentes/galvez-diario-de-pensacola/por_q.texto: It is the official Spanish account of the capture of the capital of British West Florida.

fuentes/rochambeau-memoires/titulo.texto: Military, Historical and Political Memoirs of Rochambeau

fuentes/rochambeau-memoires/autor.texto: Jean-Baptiste Donatien de Vimeur, Count of Rochambeau

fuentes/rochambeau-memoires/resumen.texto: Memoirs of the commander of the French expeditionary corps in North America. They cover the arrival at Newport in 1780, the march south with Washington, and the siege of Yorktown in September and October 1781, including the action of de Grasse's fleet.

fuentes/rochambeau-memoires/por_que_impo.texto: It is the main French source on the siege of Yorktown, written by one of its commanders.

fuentes/diarios-de-washington/resumen.texto: Six-volume edition of Washington's diaries by Donald Jackson and Dorothy Twohig. The volume covering 1771-1775 and 1780-1781 records day by day the march from New York to Virginia and the siege of Yorktown, from September 28 to October 19, 1781.

fuentes/diarios-de-washington/por_que_im.texto: They contain the American commander's entries during the siege of Yorktown.

fuentes/fletcher-v-peck/resumen.texto: Unanimous ruling of the Supreme Court of the United States, written by Chief Justice John Marshall, on the sale of lands in the Yazoo fraud. It held that Georgia's 1796 law annulling the grants of 1795 violated the Contract Clause of the Constitution, and it was the first time the Court struck down a state law.

fuentes/fletcher-v-peck/por_que_importa.texto: It settled the legal question of the Yazoo lands and established that state laws are also subject to the Constitution.

fuentes/khlebnikov-baranov/titulo.texto: Baranov: Chief Manager of the Russian Colonies in America

fuentes/khlebnikov-baranov/resumen.texto: Biography of the ruler of Russian America, written by an employee of the Russian-American Company who knew him in Sitka (Khlebnikov was there from 1818 to 1832). It covers the founding of Sitka, the war with the Tlingit in 1802-1804, dealings with the fur hunters, and the company's management. It was translated into English in 1973.

fuentes/khlebnikov-baranov/por_que_impor.texto: It is a close biography by a company employee who knew Baranov and used his papers and witnesses; it is the main source on Baranov and the Sitka wars.

fuentes/lisianski-voyage-round-the-world.texto: A Voyage Round the World in the Years 1803, 4, 5, & 6

Account by the captain of the Neva, who reached Sitka in 1804 during the war with the Tlingit. It covers the bombardment of the Tlingit fort in October 1804 and the founding of the Russian capital of New Archangel, with descriptions of the Indigenous peoples. He published it himself in Saint Petersburg in 1812; in 1814 he issued his own English translation in London, under the title A Voyage Round the World in the Years 1803, 4, 5, & 6.
It is the account of an eyewitness to the Battle of Sitka of 1804.

fuentes/edmunds-tecumseh/titulo.texto: Tecumseh and the Quest for Indian Leadership

fuentes/edmunds-tecumseh/resumen.texto: Biography of Tecumseh and of his brother Tenskwatawa, with the confederacy they built against land cessions, Tippecanoe in 1811, and Tecumseh's death on the Thames in 1813. It treats the rivalries among Indigenous leaders and the decisions of Harrison and the British.

fuentes/edmunds-tecumseh/por_que_importa.texto: It is the standard biography of Tecumseh; it challenges the image of the pan-Indian leader.

fuentes/cartas-de-harrison-esarey/titulo.texto: Messages and Letters of William Henry Harrison

fuentes/cartas-de-harrison-esarey/resume.texto: Letters from 1800 to 1814, which Logan Esarey edited in two volumes of the Indiana Historical Collections (Indianapolis, 1922): the official correspondence of the governor of Indiana Territory from 1800 to 1812 and his campaign of 1812-1814. They include the reports on Tippecanoe and the Thames.

fuentes/cartas-de-harrison-esarey/por_qu.texto: They are the reports of the man who commanded at Tippecanoe and the Thames.

fuentes/fuller-new-madrid-earthquake/res.texto: Bulletin 494 of the United States Geological Survey. It gathers the testimony from 1811-1812 and the reports of survivors, among them Eliza Bryan's letter, and describes the effects on the surface, the new lakes such as Reelfoot, and the areas that were shaken.

fuentes/fuller-new-madrid-earthquake/por.texto: It is the classic scientific study of the 1811-1812 earthquakes.

fuentes/penick-new-madrid-earthquakes/re.texto: Study of the earthquakes of December 16, 1811, and January 23 and February 7, 1812, with the testimony, the aftershocks, and the effects on frontier society. It gathers the testimony of the period.

fuentes/penick-new-madrid-earthquakes/po.texto: It is the historical monograph on the earthquakes.

fuentes/halbert-ball-creek-war/autor.texto: Henry S. Halbert and Timothy H. Ball

fuentes/halbert-ball-creek-war/resumen.texto: History of the Red Stick War with the United States, with the testimony of survivors. It narrates the attack on Fort Mims in August 1813, the campaigns of Jackson, Coffee, Floyd, and Claiborne, and the battle of Horseshoe Bend on March 27, 1814.

fuentes/halbert-ball-creek-war/por_que_i.texto: It is the first detailed history of the Creek War, based on oral testimony from the region.

fuentes/missall-seminole-wars/titulo.texto: The Seminole Wars: America's Longest Indian Conflict

fuentes/missall-seminole-wars/autor.texto: John Missall and Mary Lou Missall

fuentes/missall-seminole-wars/resumen.texto: History of the three Seminole Wars, from Jackson's incursions into Florida in 1817-1818 to the end of the third war in 1858, covering the campaigns, the removal west, and the resistance of Osceola and other leaders.

fuentes/missall-seminole-wars/por_que_im.texto: It is the standard synthesis of the three conflicts.

fuentes/fehrenbach-comanches/titulo.texto: Comanches: The Destruction of a People

fuentes/fehrenbach-comanches/resumen.texto: History of the Comanches from their arrival on the southern plains until their subjugation in 1875, seen from Texas. It covers the wars with settlers and Rangers, the Council House Fight of 1840, and the Comanche raid as far as Victoria and Linnville.

fuentes/fehrenbach-comanches/por_que_imp.texto: It is a Texas history of the Comanches, written from the settlers' point of view.

fuentes/chittenden-american-fur-trade/ti.texto: The American Fur Trade of the Far West

fuentes/chittenden-american-fur-trade/re.texto: Three-volume history of the fur trade of the Rockies and the Missouri. It covers the Ashley company, the Arikara attack of June 1823 on Ashley's boat, the expedition of Colonel Leavenworth against the Arikara villages, and dealings with the Plains peoples.

fuentes/chittenden-american-fur-trade/po.texto: It is a classic history of the fur trade, with accounts of the events of 1823.

fuentes/zanger-red-bird/resumen.texto: Chapter from the book edited by R. David Edmunds, American Indian Leaders: Studies in Diversity (University of Nebraska Press), on the Winnebago chief Red Bird and the conflict of 1827 on the upper Mississippi. It covers the murders of the Methode family (1826) and their consequences, Red Bird's attack on Registre Gagnier's cabin in Prairie du Chien and on the boats near the Bad Axe River (June 1827), Colonel Henry Atkinson's campaign, and Red Bird's surrender. It argues that Americans attributed to him a leadership he did not have.

fuentes/zanger-red-bird/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most cited study of the Winnebago conflict of 1827.

fuentes/ley-de-vacunacion-india-1832/res.texto: Act of May 5, 1832, which authorized the president to employ physicians to vaccinate Indigenous people against smallpox wherever he considered it advisable, and to pay the costs from federal funds. It is one of the first federal health laws for Indigenous peoples.

fuentes/ley-de-vacunacion-india-1832/por.texto: It is the legal basis of federal smallpox vaccination of Indigenous peoples.

fuentes/tratado-de-new-echota-1835/autor.texto: United States and the Cherokee Treaty Party

fuentes/tratado-de-new-echota-1835/resum.texto: Treaty signed on December 29, 1835, by the commissioners of the United States and a minority group of Cherokees, including Major Ridge, John Ridge, and Elias Boudinot. It ceded all Cherokee lands east of the Mississippi for five million dollars and set the removal to the West. Chief John Ross and most of the nation rejected it.

fuentes/tratado-de-new-echota-1835/por_q.texto: It was the legal basis for the expulsion of the Cherokees on the Trail of Tears, although its validity was and remains disputed.

fuentes/seattle-version-de-smith-1887/ti.texto: Henry A. Smith's Version of Chief Seattle's Speech (1887)

fuentes/seattle-version-de-smith-1887/re.texto: Text published in the Seattle Sunday Star in 1887 by the physician and poet Henry A. Smith, who says he heard Chief Seattle's speech before Governor Isaac Stevens around 1854 and reconstructed it from his notes more than thirty years later. It is the basis of all later versions.

fuentes/seattle-version-de-smith-1887/po.texto: It is the only source from which the versions of “Chief Seattle's speech” derive; scholars debate how much of it is Seattle's and how much is Smith's.

fuentes/informe-de-sand-creek-1865/titul.texto: Report of the Joint Committee on the Conduct of the War: The Massacre of the Cheyennes

fuentes/informe-de-sand-creek-1865/resum.texto: Report of Congress from 1865, with testimony from officers and civilians about the attack by Colorado volunteer troops under Colonel John Chivington on Black Kettle's camp on November 29, 1864. It concludes that Chivington planned and carried out a deliberate massacre of people who were under the government's protection.

fuentes/informe-de-sand-creek-1865/por_q.texto: It is the most important official document on Sand Creek; the committee condemned Chivington, who had already left the army.

fuentes/tratado-de-cesion-de-alaska-1867.texto: Treaty signed on March 30, 1867, by the Russian minister Eduard de Stoeckl and Secretary of State William Seward, by which the Russian Empire ceded its possessions in North America to the United States for 7.2 million dollars. The Senate ratified it on April 9.

It is the instrument of Alaska's sale; it did not consult the Indigenous peoples, and it separated the “uncivilized tribes,” subject to the laws the United States would enact, from the inhabitants who could become citizens.

fuentes/constitution-act-1867/resumen.texto: Act of the British Parliament, given royal assent on March 29, 1867, which united into a federal dominion the province of Canada, divided into Ontario and Quebec, together with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. It set the division of powers between the federal government and the provinces and took effect on July 1, 1867.

fuentes/constitution-act-1867/por_que_im.texto: It is Canada's founding document; it was called the British North America Act until 1982.

fuentes/constitution-act-1867/leer.0.tit.texto: Official text on the Government of Canada's legislation website

fuentes/creighton-road-to-confederation/.texto: The Road to Confederation: The Emergence of Canada, 1863-1867

History of the negotiations for Canadian Confederation, with the Charlottetown and Quebec conferences of 1864, the debates in the provinces, and the London talks of 1866-1867. It treats the intentions of Canadian politicians and the role of the British.
It is the classic history of the process that led to Confederation.

fuentes/thompson-army-and-the-navajo/tit.texto: The Army and the Navajo: The Bosque Redondo Reservation Experiment, 1863-1868

fuentes/thompson-army-and-the-navajo/res.texto: Study of Kit Carson's campaign against the Navajos and of the confinement of thousands of them on the Bosque Redondo Reservation at Fort Sumner, from army policy to the failure of the experiment and the treaty of 1868.

fuentes/thompson-army-and-the-navajo/por.texto: It is an academic study of the Long Walk and of Bosque Redondo from the viewpoint of army and government policy.

fuentes/bailey-the-long-walk/titulo.texto: The Long Walk: A History of the Navajo Wars, 1846-1868

fuentes/bailey-the-long-walk/resumen.texto: History of the wars between the Navajos and the United States, from the occupation of New Mexico in 1846 to the treaty of 1868, covering Carson's campaign of 1863-1864, the Long Walk, and the confinement at Bosque Redondo.

fuentes/bailey-the-long-walk/por_que_imp.texto: It is one of the first studies devoted to the Long Walk; it predates more recent works that correct it.

fuentes/articulos-de-capitulacion-de-mon.texto: Pierre de Rigaud de Vaudreuil and Jeffery Amherst

Act of 55 articles signed on September 8, 1760, by the governor general of New France and the British commander, which handed Canada over to Great Britain. It asks that the inhabitants have the rights of British subjects, and it regulates Catholic worship, the clergy, the seigneurs, the enslaved people and, in Article 40, the lands and religion of the Indigenous peoples allied with France. The British commander granted most of it, but denied the honors of war to the French troops, rejected that the King of France name the bishop and that the Jesuits, Recollets, and Sulpicians remain, and on the Acadians answered that they were already British subjects.
It is the document by which New France passed to Great Britain; its guarantees on religion, laws, and lands were later invoked for the Quebec regime and for the rights of Indigenous peoples.
English text in the collection of laws and public acts relating to Canada, printed in Quebec by P. E. Desbarats in 1824 (Canadiana)

personas/hernando-de-soto/resumen.texto: Conquistador from Extremadura who took part in the conquest of Nicaragua and Peru, where he was at Cajamarca in 1532. With his share of Peruvian wealth he obtained from Charles V the governorship of Florida, and between 1539 and 1542 he traveled with about 600 men through the chiefdoms of the present-day southeastern United States, taking maize, carriers and women; he died of fever on the Mississippi in May 1542.

personas/tascalusa/resumen.texto: Chief of a Mississippian chiefdom in present-day Alabama, described by the chroniclers of the de Soto expedition as a very tall and haughty man. Held as a hostage by de Soto, he took him to the fortified town of Mabila, where his warriors attacked the Spaniards in October 1540; what became of him after the battle is not known.

personas/pedro-menendez-de-aviles/resume.texto: Seaman from Asturias, captain general of the Indies fleet, who founded St. Augustine in 1565, took the Huguenot colony of Fort Caroline, and had some 245 shipwrecked French sailors who had surrendered executed at Matanzas. He attempted a network of forts and Jesuit missions from Florida to Chesapeake Bay and died in Santander while preparing a fleet.

personas/juan-pardo/resumen.texto: Captain sent by Menéndez de Avilés from Santa Elena who, in two expeditions (1566–1568), traveled the interior of the Carolinas and eastern Tennessee and left six forts with small garrisons, all destroyed by Indigenous people around 1568. Excavations at the Berry site in North Carolina found Fort San Juan next to the village of Joara.

personas/lucas-vazquez-de-ayllon/activo..texto: San Miguel de Gualdape (Georgia coast, uncertain site)

personas/lucas-vazquez-de-ayllon/resumen.texto: Oidor of the Audiencia of Santo Domingo whose ships captured about sixty Indigenous people on the South Carolina coast in 1521. In 1526 he took some 600 settlers, with enslaved Africans, to found San Miguel de Gualdape, the first attempt at European settlement in the mainland territory of present-day United States; he died there and the colony was abandoned within a few months.

personas/tristan-de-luna/resumen.texto: Veteran of the Coronado expedition who in 1559 took some 1,500 people to settle Pensacola Bay. A hurricane sank most of his fleet within a few weeks, and the colony was abandoned in 1561.

personas/estebanico/resumen.texto: African enslaved man born in Azemmour (Morocco), owned by Andrés Dorantes. He was one of the four survivors of the Narváez expedition who crossed the southern part of North America to reach Mexico in 1536. In 1539 he went ahead as a guide for Fray Marcos de Niza, and the Zuni of Hawikuh killed him.

personas/marcos-de-niza/resumen.texto: Franciscan born in Nice, then part of Savoy, who had been in Peru. In 1539 Viceroy Mendoza sent him north with Estebanico, and his report claimed he had seen from a distance the city of Cíbola, “greater than the city of Mexico”; when the Coronado expedition found the Zuni village of Hawikuh in 1540, the soldiers accused him of having lied.

personas/francisco-vazquez-de-coronado/r.texto: Governor of Nueva Galicia who in 1540–1542 led an expedition of some 350 Spaniards and more than a thousand Indigenous allies from central Mexico in search of the cities of Cíbola. He reached the Zuni villages, the Rio Grande and the plains of Kansas without finding riches; in the 1544 inquiry into the expedition’s abuses he was acquitted.

personas/pedro-de-castaneda-de-najera/re.texto: Soldier of the Coronado expedition, a resident of Culiacán, who some twenty years later wrote the “Relación de la jornada de Cíbola.” Beyond what his own text says, little is known about him.

personas/juan-de-onate/activo.lugar.texto: Ohkay Owingeh (San Juan de los Caballeros)

personas/juan-de-onate/resumen.texto: Son of a wealthy silver miner from Zacatecas, married to a descendant of Cortés and Moctezuma. In 1598 he brought settlers, soldiers, Franciscans and livestock to New Mexico and became its first governor; after the capture of Acoma (1599) he sentenced the men over 25 years old to amputation of a foot and to servitude. In 1614 he was convicted in Mexico for these and other abuses, among other penalties being banished from New Mexico.

personas/gaspar-perez-de-villagra/activo.texto: Ohkay Owingeh (San Juan de los Caballeros)

personas/gaspar-perez-de-villagra/resume.texto: Creole from Puebla who studied in Salamanca and was a captain and procurator of the Oñate expedition. He fought in the capture of Acoma and published in 1610 the “Historia de la Nueva México,” an epic poem in 34 cantos; in 1614 he was convicted for the execution of two deserters.

personas/pope-pueblo/resumen.texto: Tewa religious leader from Ohkay Owingeh. In 1675 he was among the 47 Pueblo men arrested and whipped for “sorcery” on the orders of Governor Treviño; from Taos he organized the revolt of August 1680. According to the testimony gathered by Otermín, he ordered the destruction of churches, images and rosaries and the abandonment of Christian names; after the victory he lost the support of the peoples and died before the Spanish returned.

personas/alonso-de-benavides/resumen.texto: Franciscan born in the Azores, custodian of the New Mexico missions from 1626 to 1629. His Memorial to the King (1630) describes the missions and the Indigenous peoples for the purposes of missionary propaganda; after meeting with her in 1631, he spread the account of the nun María de Ágreda, who was said to have preached to the Jumanos without leaving Spain.

personas/antonio-de-otermin/resumen.texto: Governor of New Mexico during the 1680 revolt. He resisted the siege of Santa Fe, evacuated the survivors to El Paso and failed in an attempt at reconquest in 1681–1682; his proceedings, with interrogations of captive Indians, are the main source on the revolt.

personas/diego-de-vargas/resumen.texto: Nobleman from Madrid, governor of New Mexico, who entered Santa Fe without combat in 1692 and in December 1693 took it by assault, after which he had some seventy defenders executed and distributed about four hundred women and children as servants. He suppressed another Pueblo revolt in 1696.

personas/gaspar-de-portola/resumen.texto: Catalan military officer, governor of the Californias, who in 1767–1768 carried out the expulsion of the Jesuits from Baja California and in 1769–1770 led the overland expedition that founded San Diego and Monterey.

personas/junipero-serra/muerte.lugar.texto: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

personas/junipero-serra/activo.lugar.texto: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

personas/junipero-serra/resumen.texto: Franciscan from Mallorca, professor of theology in Palma, who did missionary work in the Sierra Gorda of Querétaro and from 1769 in Alta California, where he founded nine missions and presided over the system until his death. In 1773 he obtained from the viceroy that the missionaries, and not the soldiers, have authority over the baptized Indians, and in a letter (1780) he defended the whipping of neophytes as a father’s punishment of his children. He was beatified in 1988 and canonized in 2015, despite opposition from California Indigenous groups.

personas/francisco-palou/resumen.texto: Franciscan from Mallorca, Serra’s disciple in Palma, who accompanied him in the Sierra Gorda and in California, where in 1776 he founded the Mission San Francisco. He wrote the “Relación histórica” of Serra’s life (1787), the basis of his later image.

personas/fermin-lasuen/muerte.lugar.texto: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

personas/fermin-lasuen/activo.lugar.texto: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

personas/fermin-lasuen/resumen.texto: Serra’s successor as president of the Alta California missions (1785–1803), he founded nine more. In 1801 he refuted in writing the accusations of the Franciscan Antonio de la Concepción Horra, who in 1798 had charged that the system treated the neophytes cruelly.

personas/toypurina/resumen.texto: Tongva woman considered a sorceress by her own people, who in October 1785 took part, with the neophyte Nicolás José, in a plan to attack Mission San Gabriel. When the plan was discovered, she was tried and banished to Mission San Carlos, where she was baptized and married a Spanish soldier; the most quoted line of her testimony, against those who lived on her land, comes from a 1958 novelized version and not from the case file.

personas/juan-bautista-de-anza/resumen.texto: Creole military officer from Sonora who opened an overland route to California in 1774 and in 1775–1776 led about 240 settlers who founded San Francisco. As governor of New Mexico he defeated the Comanche chief Cuerno Verde in 1779, and in 1786 he signed a peace with the Comanches with Ecueracapa.

personas/bernardo-de-galvez/resumen.texto: Governor of Spanish Louisiana who, in the American War of Independence, took Baton Rouge, Mobile and Pensacola from the British (1779–1781). As viceroy of New Spain he signed the “Instrucción” of 1786 for the northern frontier, which ordered war against hostile Apaches and made those who asked for peace dependent through gifts, alcohol and poor-quality weapons.

personas/jacques-cartier/resumen.texto: Navigator from Saint-Malo who made three voyages to the Gulf and the Saint Lawrence River (1534, 1535–1536 and 1541–1542). He reached the Iroquoian villages of Stadacona and Hochelaga, took the chief Donnacona and nine others to France, where they died, and spread the name “Canada,” from the Iroquoian word for village.

personas/donnacona/resumen.texto: Chief of the Iroquoian village of Stadacona, on the site of present-day Quebec City. Cartier took two of his sons to France in 1534 and him, with nine others, in 1536; he died in France around 1539 without having returned.

personas/samuel-de-champlain/resumen.texto: Navigator and cartographer from Brouage who founded Quebec in 1608 and governed it until his death, except during the English occupation of 1629–1632. He allied with the Montagnais, Algonquins and Hurons against the Iroquois League and in 1609 killed two Mohawk chiefs with his arquebus by the lake that bears his name; his accounts and maps are a basic source on the peoples of the Saint Lawrence and the Great Lakes.

personas/gabriel-sagard/resumen.texto: Lay brother of the Recollects who lived among the Hurons in 1623–1624. His “Grand voyage du pays des Hurons” (1632) describes his life, beliefs and wars and includes a dictionary of the Huron language.

personas/paul-le-jeune/resumen.texto: Superior of the Jesuits in New France from 1632, who began the annual series of the Relations. He spent the winter of 1633–1634 with a band of Montagnais (Innu) to learn their language and recounted it in the 1634 Relation, one of the most detailed descriptions of a northern hunting people.

personas/jean-de-brebeuf/resumen.texto: Jesuit from Normandy who lived among the Hurons from 1626, learned their language, wrote a catechism in it and drafted parts of the Relations. The Iroquois captured him during the destruction of the Huron villages in March 1649, and he died under ritual torture; he was canonized in 1930 among the “Canadian Martyrs.”

personas/marie-de-l-incarnation/resumen.texto: Ursuline from Tours, a widow and mother of a son, who arrived in Quebec in 1639 and founded the Ursuline convent and school for French and Indigenous girls. She wrote dictionaries and catechisms in Algonquin, Montagnais and Iroquois, now lost, and thousands of letters, of which her son published a selection in 1681; she was canonized in 2014.

personas/francois-de-laval/resumen.texto: First bishop of Quebec (apostolic vicar from 1658 and bishop from 1674), who founded the Seminary of Quebec in 1663. He fought the sale of alcohol to Indigenous people with excommunications, in conflict with governors and merchants.

personas/kateri-tekakwitha/resumen.texto: Mohawk woman, daughter of a Christian Algonquin, who as a child survived a smallpox epidemic with her face scarred. Baptized by the Jesuits in 1676, she moved to the Kahnawake mission near Montreal, where she practiced extreme penances and died at 24; she was canonized in 2012, the first Indigenous person from present-day United States or Canada to be raised to the altars as a saint.

personas/jacques-marquette/resumen.texto: French Jesuit who did missionary work among the Hurons and Odawas of the Great Lakes and in 1673 traveled the Mississippi with Louis Jolliet as far as the mouth of the Arkansas. He died in 1675 on his way back from a mission among the Illinois.

personas/louis-jolliet/resumen.texto: Merchant and cartographer born in Quebec and educated by the Jesuits, who in 1673 traveled the Mississippi with Marquette and confirmed that it flowed into the Gulf of Mexico.

personas/la-salle/resumen.texto: Merchant and explorer from Rouen who in 1682 descended the Mississippi to the Gulf and took possession of its entire basin for Louis XIV, naming it Louisiana. In 1685 he landed by mistake on the Texas coast with about 300 settlers, and he was murdered by his own men in 1687.

personas/kondiaronk/resumen.texto: Wendat (Huron-Petun) chief of Michilimackinac, called “Le Rat” by the French. He was one of the main negotiators of the Great Peace of Montreal and died there during the 1701 conferences. Baron de Lahontan took him as the model of the Indigenous person who criticizes Europe in his “Dialogues” (1703), though how faithfully they reflect his ideas is doubtful.

personas/bienville/resumen.texto: Born in Montreal, he was governor of French Louisiana in several periods and founded New Orleans in 1718. Under his government the Code Noir of Louisiana (1724) was enacted, and the wars against the Natchez and the Chickasaws were fought.

personas/le-page-du-pratz/resumen.texto: French colonist who lived for about eight years near the Natchez before the 1729 rebellion and learned their language. His “Histoire de la Louisiane” (1758) describes their society, religion and the human sacrifices at the funerals of the nobility.

personas/jacques-le-moyne/resumen.texto: Huguenot painter who was at Fort Caroline and escaped in 1565. Theodor de Bry published engravings in 1591 based on his drawings of the Timucua, together with his account; only one original painting of Florida survives, and the fidelity of the engravings is disputed.

personas/rene-de-laudonniere/resumen.texto: Huguenot who founded Fort Caroline in 1564, on the land of the Timucua chief Saturiwa, and survived the Spanish attack of 1565. His “Histoire notable de la Floride” (1586) narrates the colony and its relations with the Timucua chiefs.

personas/jean-ribault/resumen.texto: Huguenot navigator from Dieppe who in 1562 built Charlesfort at Port Royal and in 1565 brought reinforcements to Fort Caroline. His fleet was wrecked in a hurricane as he was about to attack St. Augustine, and Menéndez de Avilés had him executed at Matanzas along with most of his men.

personas/richard-hakluyt/resumen.texto: English clergyman and geographer who gathered travel accounts in “The Principall Navigations” (1589) and in 1584 wrote a discourse for the queen in favor of colonizing North America, with religious, commercial and rivalry-with-Spain arguments, whose cruelty toward the Indians he cited according to Las Casas.

personas/thomas-hariot/resumen.texto: Mathematician and astronomer in the service of Walter Raleigh who was at Roanoke in 1585–1586, learned part of the Carolina Algonquian language with Manteo and Wanchese, and wrote the “Briefe and True Report” (1588). In 1609 he drew the Moon as observed through a telescope, months before Galileo.

personas/john-white-pintor/resumen.texto: English painter and cartographer who accompanied the 1585 expedition and left dozens of watercolors of the Carolina Algonquians, the most important visual source on them. He was governor of the colony from 1587; when he returned in 1590 he found it abandoned.

personas/powhatan/resumen.texto: Paramount chief of a confederacy of some thirty Algonquian-speaking communities on the Virginia coast, which he had inherited and expanded through conquest; according to William Strachey he had the Chesapeake destroyed around 1607. He traded and fought with the English of Jamestown; the marriage of his daughter Pocahontas to John Rolfe (1614) opened a truce that lasted until his death.

personas/pocahontas/resumen.texto: Daughter of Powhatan. In 1613 the English took her hostage to negotiate with her father; in captivity she was baptized with the name Rebecca and in 1614 she married the colonist John Rolfe. She traveled to England in 1616 as propaganda for the Virginia Company and died in Gravesend in 1617, as she was beginning the return voyage.

personas/opechancanough/resumen.texto: Brother or relative of Powhatan and his de facto successor, who led the coordinated attacks of 1622 and 1644 against the Virginia colonists. Captured in 1646 when very old, he was shot by a soldier while in custody in Jamestown.

personas/john-smith/resumen.texto: English soldier who had fought against the Ottomans, a member of the Jamestown council and its president in 1608–1609. He mapped Chesapeake Bay and obtained maize from the Powhatan through barter and threats. The scene in which Pocahontas saves his life is not in his 1608 account: it appears in a letter he wrote in 1616 to Queen Anne, which he himself published in the “Generall Historie” of 1624; historians debate whether it happened or was an adoption rite that he did not understand.

personas/squanto/resumen.texto: Patuxet captured in 1614 by the English captain Thomas Hunt and sold as a slave in Málaga; he went to England and returned to New England in 1619, when the epidemic had emptied his village. He served as interpreter for the Plymouth colonists and as mediator with Massasoit until his death from fever in 1622.

personas/massasoit/resumen.texto: Principal sachem of the Wampanoag, whose people had been decimated by the 1616–1619 epidemic. In March 1621 he signed with the Plymouth colonists an alliance of mutual aid, partly against the Narragansetts, his rivals, which he maintained until his death.

personas/metacom/muerte.lugar.texto: Rhode Island and Providence Plantations colony

personas/metacom/resumen.texto: Son of Massasoit and sachem of the Wampanoag from 1662, called “King Philip” by the English. He led the 1675–1676 war against the New England colonies; he died in August 1676 at the hands of an Indigenous man allied with the English, his head was displayed in Plymouth for about twenty years, and his nine-year-old son was sold into slavery outside the colony.

personas/uncas/resumen.texto: Mohegan sachem, separate from the Pequots, who allied with the English in the Pequot War and fought at Mystic. In 1643 he captured the Narragansett sachem Miantonomi and executed him with the approval of the colonial commissioners; he was also an ally of Connecticut in King Philip’s War.

personas/john-sassamon/resumen.texto: Christian Massachusett, interpreter for John Eliot and for a time a student at Harvard, who became a scribe for Metacom. In January 1675 he was found dead in a frozen pond after warning Plymouth that Metacom was preparing war; the execution of three Wampanoag for his death precipitated King Philip’s War.

personas/william-bradford/resumen.texto: English Separatist who arrived on the Mayflower and governed the Plymouth colony almost without interruption from 1621 to 1657. His history “Of Plymouth Plantation” narrates the colony up to 1647, including the alliance with Massasoit and the Pequot War.

personas/john-winthrop/resumen.texto: Puritan lawyer who led the 1630 fleet of the Massachusetts Bay Company and served as its governor for twelve years. In a 1634 letter he interpreted the deaths of Indigenous people from smallpox as a way in which God clarified the colonists’ title to the land.

personas/john-mason/resumen.texto: English soldier, a veteran of the Dutch wars, who led the Connecticut forces in the Pequot War and burned the Mystic fort in May 1637. His account of the war, written around 1656, was published in 1736.

personas/john-underhill/resumen.texto: Massachusetts captain who took part in the attack on Mystic and justified it in “Newes from America” (1638). He later served the Dutch in Kieft’s War and in 1644 led the massacre of an Indigenous village near Pound Ridge.

personas/roger-williams/resumen.texto: Puritan minister banished from Massachusetts in 1635, among other reasons for holding that the king’s charter did not give a right to Indian land unless it was bought from them. He founded Providence on land ceded by the Narragansetts, defended the separation of church and state, and published “A Key into the Language of America” in 1643.

personas/john-eliot/resumen.texto: Puritan minister of Roxbury who learned the Massachusett language with Indigenous interpreters, preached in it from 1646, and from 1651 organized the “praying towns” of Christian Indians. With the Indigenous translators and printers John Sassamon, Job Nesutan and James Printer he published the complete Bible in Massachusett (1663), the first printed in the Americas, and a grammar (1666).

personas/caleb-cheeshahteaumuck/resumen.texto: Wampanoag from Martha’s Vineyard, the first Indigenous graduate of Harvard, in 1665. He died of tuberculosis the following year; a letter of his in Latin from 1663, addressed to English benefactors, survives.

personas/mary-rowlandson/resumen.texto: Wife of the minister of Lancaster (Massachusetts), captured in the February 1676 attack during King Philip’s War. She spent eleven weeks with Narragansetts, Nipmucs and Wampanoag until she was ransomed for twenty pounds; her narrative (1682) inaugurated the New England captivity literature.

personas/nathaniel-bacon/resumen.texto: Recently arrived landowner in Virginia who in 1676 led a rebellion of settlers against Governor Berkeley, demanding war against all Indigenous peoples; his men also attacked peoples allied with the colony. He burned Jamestown in September and died of dysentery in October 1676.

personas/william-penn/resumen.texto: English Quaker who in 1681 received the charter of Pennsylvania from Charles II in payment of a debt owed to his father. He bought the land occupied by the Lenape with deeds, and in 1681 wrote to them that he wished to enjoy that land with their love and consent and to live with them as neighbors and friends; in 1737 his sons used a dubious deed for the “Walking Purchase.”

personas/peter-minuit/resumen.texto: Director of New Netherland (1626–1631), to whom the purchase of Manhattan from the Lenape in 1626 is attributed. In 1638 he founded New Sweden in the service of Sweden, and he died that year in a hurricane in the Caribbean.

personas/willem-kieft/resumen.texto: Director of New Netherland who in 1639 sought to collect tribute from neighboring peoples and in February 1643 ordered the night attacks on Lenape refugees at Pavonia and Corlears Hook, with about 120 dead. The war that followed ruined the colony; he died in the shipwreck of the vessel that was carrying him to render an account.

personas/eleazar-wheelock/resumen.texto: Congregationalist minister from Connecticut who in 1754 opened the Moor's Charity School for young Indigenous people, among them Joseph Brant. With the money Samson Occom raised in Great Britain he founded Dartmouth College in 1769, where white students soon outnumbered Indigenous ones.

personas/samson-occom/resumen.texto: Mohegan from Connecticut, a student of Wheelock and a Presbyterian minister, who in 1766–1768 preached in Great Britain and raised some 12,000 pounds for the education of Indigenous people. He broke with Wheelock when the latter used that money for Dartmouth; in 1772 he published a widely circulated sermon, and in 1785 he founded the Indigenous Christian community of Brothertown, in New York.

personas/william-johnson/resumen.texto: Irishman who made a fortune as a trader in the Mohawk Valley, learned the language and was adopted by the Mohawk. As British superintendent of Indian affairs for the north (1756–1774) he conducted diplomacy with the Six Nations, made peace with Pontiac and negotiated the Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1768); he had eight children with the Mohawk woman Molly Brant.

personas/pontiac/resumen.texto: Odawa war leader of the Detroit region who in May 1763 laid siege to the British fort, in an uprising that bears his name although many peoples with leaders of their own took part. He made peace with William Johnson in 1766 and was assassinated in 1769 by a Peoria man in Cahokia.

personas/jeffery-amherst/resumen.texto: British commander in chief in North America, who took Louisbourg (1758) and Montreal (1760). After the war he cut the gifts and gunpowder given to Indigenous peoples, one of the causes of the 1763 rebellion, and during that war he proposed in a letter to Bouquet spreading smallpox among the rebels.

personas/henry-bouquet/resumen.texto: Swiss officer in British service who in August 1763 defeated Delawares, Shawnees and Mingos at Bushy Run and lifted the siege of Fort Pitt. In his July 1763 letters with Amherst he accepted the idea of spreading smallpox with blankets; in 1764 he forced the peoples of the Ohio to return hundreds of white captives.

personas/william-trent/resumen.texto: Pennsylvania fur trader and militia captain at Fort Pitt during the 1763 siege. His diary records that on June 24 two Delaware envoys were given two blankets and a handkerchief from the smallpox hospital, in the hope that they would have “the desired effect.”

personas/benjamin-franklin/resumen.texto: Printer, scientist and politician from Philadelphia, who printed the treaty minutes with the Iroquois and in a 1751 letter cited the union of the Six Nations as an example for the colonies. In 1764 he denounced the massacre of the Conestoga by the Paxton Boys; he signed the Declaration of Independence and negotiated the Treaty of Paris of 1783.

personas/logan-mingo/resumen.texto: Cayuga orator and war leader, son of Shikellamy, who settled in Ohio among the Mingo and until then had been a friend of the colonists. In 1774 Virginia settlers killed his family at Yellow Creek; he avenged them with raids and refused to make peace, with a message that Jefferson published in 1785. The exact text, its authorship and its accusation against Michael Cresap have been disputed ever since.

personas/joseph-brant/resumen.texto: Mohawk educated at Wheelock's school and protégé of William Johnson, who lived with his sister Molly Brant. He fought on the British side in the War of Independence, translated the Gospel of Mark into Mohawk and in 1784 led the loyalist Mohawk to lands on the Grand River, in present-day Ontario.

personas/george-washington/resumen.texto: Virginia planter and slaveholder whose 1754 clash with a French party began the French and Indian War. He commanded the Continental Army and in 1779 ordered the Sullivan Expedition against the Iroquois; in 1790 Seneca chiefs reminded him that this was why they called him “destroyer of villages.” As first president (1789–1797) he oversaw the Northwest War and the policy of “civilization” of Indigenous people.

personas/thomas-jefferson/resumen.texto: Virginia planter and slaveholder, drafter of the Declaration of Independence and third president (1801–1809). In “Notes on the State of Virginia” he defended the capacities of Indigenous Americans against Buffon and published Logan's speech; as president he bought Louisiana (1803) and proposed moving to the west of the Mississippi those peoples who did not accept agriculture and the cession of land.

personas/david-zeisberger/resumen.texto: Moravian missionary born in Moravia who worked for more than sixty years with the Lenape, wrote grammars and dictionaries of Lenape and Onondaga, and founded the Christian villages of Schoenbrunn and Gnadenhutten in Ohio (1772). In 1781 the British arrested him and moved his converts.

personas/little-turtle/resumen.texto: Miami war leader who, with the Shawnee Blue Jacket, defeated the armies of Harmar (1790) and St. Clair (1791). After Fallen Timbers he signed the Treaty of Greenville (1795) and from then on defended peace with the United States and the adoption of agriculture.

personas/tecumseh/resumen.texto: Shawnee leader who, with his brother Tenskwatawa, from 1808 gathered a confederation of peoples at Prophetstown to halt land cessions, on the idea that the land was common to all Indigenous peoples and that no people could sell it separately. He allied with the British in the War of 1812 and died at the Battle of the Thames in October 1813.

personas/tenskwatawa/resumen.texto: The Shawnee “Prophet,” brother of Tecumseh, who from 1805 preached the rejection of alcohol and of white customs and the persecution of Indigenous “sorcerers,” several of whom were executed by his followers. His prestige collapsed after the defeat at Tippecanoe (1811).

personas/sequoyah/resumen.texto: Cherokee silversmith who could not read in any language and who between 1809 and 1821 invented a syllabary of 86 characters (today 85) for Cherokee, which he made known in 1821 and which the nation officially adopted in 1825. He died in Mexico around 1843, while searching for Cherokees who had emigrated.

personas/john-ross-cherokee/resumen.texto: Principal chief of the Cherokee Nation from 1828 to 1866, of Scottish father and a mother from a mixed-race Cherokee family. He led his nation's legal defense before the Supreme Court and Congress, rejected the Treaty of New Echota and directed the last stage of the removal of 1838–1839.

personas/andrew-jackson/resumen.texto: General and slaveholding planter from Tennessee who defeated the Creek “Red Sticks” at Horseshoe Bend (1814) and imposed the Treaty of Fort Jackson, which ceded some 9 million hectares, also from Creeks who had been his allies. As president (1829–1837) he promoted the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and did not enforce the ruling in Worcester v. Georgia.

personas/john-marshall/resumen.texto: Chief Justice of the United States Supreme Court from 1801 to 1835. His rulings of 1823, 1831 and 1832 established that Indigenous peoples were “domestic dependent nations” with a right of occupancy over their lands, which they could sell only to the federal government, and that they were outside the reach of state laws.

personas/peter-burnett/resumen.texto: First governor of the state of California (1849–1851). In his message to the legislature in January 1851 he said that the “war of extermination” between the races should be expected to continue until the extinction of the Indian race, and that preventing it was beyond the reach of government.

personas/vitus-bering/resumen.texto: Danish naval officer in the service of Russia who in 1728 crossed the strait that bears his name and in July 1741 sighted the coast of Alaska. On the return voyage he was shipwrecked on Bering Island, where he died of scurvy.

personas/georg-steller/resumen.texto: German naturalist on Bering's expedition, who landed on Kayak Island in July 1741 and for the first time described the flora and fauna of the Alaskan coast, including the sea cow that bears his name and was extinct a few decades later. His journal is the main source for the voyage.

personas/grigori-shelikhov/resumen.texto: Fur merchant from Rylsk who in 1784 founded the first permanent Russian settlement in America, on Kodiak Island. That year his men attacked the Alutiiq refugees at Awa'uq, and he took hostage the children of the island's families; his company became the basis of the Russian-American Company.

personas/alexander-baranov/resumen.texto: Merchant who managed Shelikhov's company in Alaska from 1790 and was the first manager of the Russian-American Company until 1818. He organized otter hunting with Aleut and Alutiiq hunters who were forced to serve in rotation, retook Sitka from the Tlingit in 1804, and under his direction Fort Ross was founded in California (1812).

personas/lewis-cass/resumen.texto: Governor of the Michigan Territory (1813–1831) and Secretary of War under Jackson (1831–1836). He negotiated treaties under which the peoples of the region ceded lands, such as the Treaty of Fort Meigs (1817); in 1830 he argued in an article that Indigenous people could not be civilized and had to be moved west, and as Secretary of War he applied the removal law.

personas/thomas-paine/resumen.texto: English pamphleteer who arrived in Philadelphia in 1774. His pamphlet “Common Sense” (January 1776) argued for the independence of the colonies and republican government, and the series “The American Crisis” (1776–1783) sustained the morale of Washington's soldiers.

personas/john-c-calhoun/resumen.texto: Secretary of War under Monroe (1817–1825) and vice president (1825–1832). In 1824 he created the Bureau of Indian Affairs within the War Department, whose first head was Thomas McKenney. A slaveholder, he later became one of the main defenders of slavery, which he called “a positive good,” and of states' rights.

personas/henry-hudson/resumen.texto: English navigator. In 1609, in the service of the Dutch East India Company, he searched for the Northwest Passage aboard the “Halve Maen” and sailed up the river that now bears his name, which served as the basis for the Dutch claim to New Netherland. In 1610–1611, for English merchants, he entered Hudson Bay; in June 1611 the crew mutinied and set him adrift in a boat with his son and seven others, according to the account of the mutineer Abacuk Pricket, the only version there is, and nothing more was heard of them.

personas/samuel-adams/resumen.texto: Boston politician, organizer of the opposition to British taxes and of the Boston Committee of Correspondence (1772). He signed the Declaration of Independence and was governor of Massachusetts (1794–1797).

personas/john-jay/resumen.texto: New York politician, president of the Continental Congress (1778–1779) and one of the negotiators of the Treaty of Paris of 1783. He was the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court (1789–1795), and he negotiated with Great Britain the treaty that bears his name (1794), under which the British were to evacuate the forts of the Northwest.

personas/davy-crockett/muerte.lugar.texto: Mission San Antonio de Valero (the Alamo)

personas/davy-crockett/resumen.texto: Hunter and politician from Tennessee. He served as a scout for the Tennessee militia in the Creek War (1813–1814) under Jackson; as a congressman he opposed the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and lost his reelection in 1831. He died at the Alamo, in the Texas war, on 6 March 1836; the circumstances of his death are disputed.

personas/patrick-henry/resumen.texto: Virginia lawyer and politician. His resolutions of 1765 against the Stamp Act and his speech of March 1775 (“Give me liberty, or give me death,” whose text was reconstructed decades later from witness accounts) made him a figure of independence. He was governor of Virginia (1776–1779 and 1784–1786). He owned slaves all his life; in 1773 he wrote that slavery was an evil but that he was held back by “the general inconvenience of living without them.”

personas/phillis-wheatley/resumen.texto: Poet born in West Africa (probably in present-day Gambia or Senegal) and taken to Boston as a slave in 1761. Her book “Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral” (London, 1773) was the first book of poetry published by an African American; the Wheatleys freed her shortly afterward.

personas/john-hancock/resumen.texto: Boston merchant and politician. He presided over the Continental Congress (1775–1777), was the first to sign the Declaration of Independence and governed Massachusetts (1780–1785 and 1787–1793).

personas/benedict-arnold/resumen.texto: Connecticut officer. In 1775 he took part in the capture of Fort Ticonderoga and led the expedition against Quebec through Maine, where he was wounded; he fought at Saratoga (1777). In 1780, as commander of West Point, he defected to the British, in whose army he became a general.

personas/meriwether-lewis/resumen.texto: Army captain and secretary to Jefferson. With William Clark he led (1804–1806) the expedition that, from St. Louis, explored the lands of the Louisiana Purchase to the Pacific and returned, with the help of interpreters such as Sacagawea. He was governor of the Louisiana Territory (1807–1809) and died of a gunshot wound in Tennessee; most historians classify his death as suicide, and some dispute this.

personas/anne-bradstreet/resumen.texto: English Puritan poet who arrived in Massachusetts in 1630. Her book “The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America” (London, 1650) was the first published by a poet from the English colonies of North America.

personas/peter-stuyvesant/resumen.texto: Director-general of New Netherland (1647–1664). In 1655 he took New Sweden; in 1657 he prohibited, under penalty of fine and imprisonment, lodging Quakers, and he tried to prevent the residence of Jewish refugees; in 1664 he surrendered the colony to an English fleet, which renamed it New York. During his government the colony expanded the use of the Company's slaves, and there were the Peach War (1655) and the Esopus Wars (1659–1663).

personas/jonathan-edwards/resumen.texto: Congregationalist theologian of the Great Awakening and author of “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God” (1741). Minister of Northampton until 1750, he then lived in Stockbridge as a missionary to the Mohicans, and there he wrote “Freedom of the Will” (1754). He owned slaves.

personas/juan-rodriguez-cabrillo/resumen.texto: Navigator in the service of Spain whose nationality (Portuguese or Castilian) is disputed. He left Navidad (New Spain) in 1542, entered San Diego Bay on 28 September, and continued north along the coast of California. He died on 3 January 1543 of an infected wound after a fracture, and his pilot Bartolomé Ferrer brought the ships back.

personas/james-wolfe/resumen.texto: British general who took part in the siege of Louisbourg (1758) and in 1759 commanded the army that attacked Quebec. He died in the Battle of the Plains of Abraham, on 13 September 1759.

personas/daniel-boone/resumen.texto: Explorer and settler of Kentucky. In 1775, hired by the Transylvania Company, which had bought from the Cherokees their claim to Kentucky at Sycamore Shoals (a private purchase that the Proclamation of 1763 and the laws of Virginia and North Carolina prohibited, that Dragging Canoe rejected, and that Virginia annulled in 1778), he opened the road through the Cumberland Gap that would become the Wilderness Road, and founded Boonesborough. Captured by the Shawnees in 1778 and adopted among them (according to tradition, into the family of Blackfish), he escaped; in 1799 he moved to Spanish Louisiana, where he was syndic of the Femme Osage district.

personas/winfield-scott/resumen.texto: General of the United States Army. In 1832 he signed the Black Hawk Purchase with Sauk and Fox chiefs; in 1836 he commanded operations against the Seminoles, and in 1838 he directed the forced removal of the Cherokees to the west, for which his troops gathered them into internment camps. In mid-1838 he accepted John Ross's plan and let the Cherokee council conduct the rest of the removal.

personas/john-harvard/resumen.texto: English minister who arrived in Charlestown (Massachusetts) in 1637 and died of tuberculosis the following year. He left the college founded in 1636 half of his property and his library, and the college took his name in 1639.

personas/anne-hutchinson/resumen.texto: English colonist who, in the Antinomian Controversy (1636–1638), challenged the doctrine of the Massachusetts ministers. Convicted of heresy and banished in 1637–1638, she founded Portsmouth (Rhode Island) with her followers; in August 1643, already in Dutch territory, she and six of her children and others of her household were killed by Siwanoys during Kieft's War.

personas/william-clark/resumen.texto: Officer who co-led with Meriwether Lewis the 1804–1806 expedition to the Pacific. He was governor of the Missouri Territory (1813–1820) and superintendent of Indian Affairs in St. Louis (1822–1838), a post from which he negotiated land cession treaties with peoples of the region.

personas/cotton-mather/resumen.texto: Puritan minister of Boston and author of some 400 works, among them the church history “Magnalia Christi Americana” (1702). He defended the Salem witch trials of 1692–1693 in “Wonders of the Invisible World,” although he held no office on the court: he advised the judges (in “The Return of Several Ministers” he asked for caution with spectral evidence while also urging that prosecutions continue) and, according to Robert Calef, at the execution of George Burroughs he calmed the crowd so that the executions could go on; historians disagree about his weight. In 1721 he promoted inoculation against smallpox, which he had learned of through Onesimus, a slave of his.

personas/john-dickinson/resumen.texto: Lawyer from Philadelphia and Delaware. His “Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania” (1767–1768) rejected the Townshend duties; in 1776 he opposed declaring independence and did not sign the Declaration, although he had drafted the first version of the Articles of Confederation.

personas/george-mason/resumen.texto: Virginia planter who drafted the Virginia Declaration of Rights (June 1776). In 1787 he refused to sign the federal Constitution, among other reasons for the lack of a bill of rights; he owned slaves and criticized the slave trade.

personas/nathanael-greene/resumen.texto: General of the Continental Army. Quartermaster General (1778–1780) and then commander of the Southern Army (1780–1783), with which, without winning the great pitched battles, he wore down Cornwallis in the Carolinas and recovered Charleston, which the British evacuated at the end of 1782.

personas/henry-knox/resumen.texto: Boston bookseller and chief of artillery of the Continental Army, who in the winter of 1775–1776 brought to Boston the cannon captured at Ticonderoga. He was Secretary of War of the Confederation (1785–1789) and of Washington (1789–1794): he handled Indian affairs, proposed dealing with the Indian nations through treaties and land purchases, and directed the operations of the Northwest Indian War.

personas/osceola/resumen.texto: Seminole warrior, born as Billy Powell in a Creek village, son of a Muscogee mother. He opposed the westward removal provided for in the Treaty of Payne's Landing and was a leading figure in the Second Seminole War (1835–1842). General Thomas Jesup captured him in October 1837 at a peace meeting under a white flag; he died as a prisoner, of illness, at Fort Moultrie. On 28 December 1835 he had killed at Fort King the agent Wiley Thompson, who had deposed the chiefs opposed to removal and had held him prisoner; that attack and the ambush of Dade's column the same day opened the Second Seminole War.

personas/kazimierz-pulaski/resumen.texto: Polish nobleman who fought in the Confederation of Bar and, in exile, arrived in America in 1777. He distinguished himself at Brandywine, organized a legion of cavalry and infantry, and died of a wound received at the siege of Savannah (October 1779).

personas/richard-henry-lee/resumen.texto: Virginia politician who on 7 June 1776 presented to the Continental Congress the resolution that the united colonies “are, and of right ought to be, free and independent states,” and signed the Declaration. In 1787–1788 he opposed ratifying the Constitution without a bill of rights.

personas/friedrich-wilhelm-von-steuben/r.texto: Prussian officer who arrived in America at the end of 1777. At Valley Forge (winter of 1777–1778) he trained the Continental Army in a common drill, which he later set down in a regulation (1779), and he was inspector general of the army.

personas/horatio-gates/resumen.texto: Retired British officer, settled in Virginia, who commanded the Northern Army when Burgoyne surrendered at Saratoga (October 1777), a victory whose credit is disputed with Arnold and Daniel Morgan. He was defeated by Cornwallis at Camden (South Carolina) on 16 August 1780.

personas/stephen-f-austin/resumen.texto: Empresario who carried on the project of his father, Moses Austin, authorized by Spain, and from 1821, with the permission of the Mexican government, settled some 300 Anglo-American families on the Brazos, the “Old Three Hundred,” many with slaves; he worked to keep slavery legal in Texas despite the opposition of the Mexican government. The colony settled on Karankawa lands at the mouths of the Colorado and the Brazos; after the clashes of 1823 (at Skull Creek the militia killed 19), Austin wrote that they had to be exterminated, and in 1825 he ordered them pursued and killed, a policy that historians such as Kelly F. Himmel (“The Conquest of the Karankawas and the Tonkawas,” 1999) describe as extermination. After his imprisonment in Mexico (1834–1835) he supported the Texas war: he commanded the Texan forces at the siege of Béxar (1835) and was commissioner to the United States.

personas/zebulon-pike/resumen.texto: Officer of the United States Army. In 1806–1807 he led an expedition toward the headwaters of the Arkansas and Red rivers; Spanish authorities captured him on 26 February 1807 in the south of present-day Colorado, took him to Santa Fe and Chihuahua, and released him on the Louisiana frontier. His 1810 report described New Mexico and Texas. Historians debate whether the expedition was also a military reconnaissance of those provinces commissioned by General James Wilkinson, who was at the same time a paid agent of Spain. He died at the Battle of York (1813).

personas/louis-joseph-de-montcalm/resume.texto: Commander of the French regular troops in New France from 1756. He took Oswego (1756) and Fort William Henry (1757), and died on 14 September 1759 of wounds received in the Battle of the Plains of Abraham.

personas/wouter-van-twiller/resumen.texto: Director of New Netherland (1633–1637), nephew of Kiliaen van Rensselaer. He bought Governors Island from the Canarsee and failed to dislodge the New England colonists from the Connecticut valley; he was dismissed in 1637 after complaints from the officer Lubbert van Dincklagen, and was succeeded by Willem Kieft.

personas/sebastiaen-jansen-krol/resumen.texto: Comforter of the sick for the Dutch West India Company, he arrived in New Netherland in 1624 and was commander of Fort Orange. In 1630 he arranged the purchase of the Rensselaerswyck lands and led the colony in 1632–1633, between Minuit and Van Twiller.

personas/willem-verhulst/resumen.texto: Employee of the Dutch West India Company, provisional director of New Netherland in 1625–1626, before Minuit. The site of Fort Amsterdam, at the tip of Manhattan, was decided during his administration; unpopular among the colonists, he was dismissed and expelled from the colony in 1626, after a trial to which the council subjected him and his wife, and he returned to the Netherlands with the news that Manhattan had been bought for goods valued at 60 guilders. Some historians attribute that purchase to him, which the traditional version assigns to Minuit. Nothing more is known of his life.

personas/alejandro-o-reilly/resumen.texto: Lieutenant general of the Spanish army, born in Ireland. In 1769 he led the expedition that restored Spanish authority in Louisiana after the 1768 rebellion against Governor Ulloa: he had five or six Creole ringleaders executed, depending on the source, and banished others. He prohibited the trade in enslaved Indigenous people and abolished their enslavement in the colony, and he allowed enslaved people to buy their freedom.

personas/luis-de-unzaga/resumen.texto: Governor of Spanish Louisiana from late 1769 to 1777; later captain general of Venezuela and of Cuba. He tolerated a more open trade than the rules set, and in 1776–1777 he secretly sent gunpowder from the royal storehouses, by way of the Mississippi and the Ohio, to the rebel forces in Virginia, which reached Fort Pitt.

personas/esteban-rodriguez-miro/resumen.texto: Spanish officer who accompanied Gálvez in the West Florida campaigns (1779–1781) and was acting governor (1782) and titular governor (1785–1791) of Louisiana and West Florida. Facing the United States, which claimed the 31st parallel, he defended the more northerly Spanish boundary (32° 28′, with Natchez), and in 1790 he fortified Nogales (today Vicksburg); in 1787 he received the secret loyalty of James Wilkinson of Kentucky, and in 1788 he organized aid after the fire that destroyed nearly all of New Orleans.

personas/henry-laurens/resumen.texto: Charleston slave trader and rice planter, vice president of South Carolina in 1776-1777, and president of the Continental Congress from November 1, 1777, to December 9, 1778, the period in which the Articles of Confederation were approved. Sent to the Netherlands, he was captured at sea by the British in 1780 and held in the Tower of London until December 31, 1781, when he was exchanged for Cornwallis. He never freed his roughly 260 enslaved people.

personas/samuel-huntington/resumen.texto: Connecticut lawyer and judge, signer of the Declaration of Independence and of the Articles of Confederation. He succeeded John Jay as president of the Continental Congress on September 28, 1779, and resigned due to illness on July 9, 1781, so he also presided when the Articles took effect; that is why he is sometimes cited as the first president of the Congress of the Confederation. He was governor of Connecticut from 1786 until his death.

personas/thomas-mckean/resumen.texto: Delaware lawyer, delegate to Congress, and signer of the Declaration of Independence and of the Articles of Confederation. He was elected president of Congress when Huntington resigned, after Samuel Johnston declined the office, and he held it from July 10 to November 4, 1781; he resigned on learning of the British surrender at Yorktown, but Congress asked him to stay until the next session began. He was also president of Delaware for one month in 1777, chief justice of Pennsylvania, and its second governor.

personas/john-hanson/resumen.texto: Maryland merchant and politician, delegate to Congress from 1779. He signed the Articles of Confederation in 1781, when Maryland ratified them, and presided over Congress for one year from November 1781. He was not the first president under the Articles (he was preceded by Huntington and McKean), but some of his descendants and biographers claimed otherwise and presented him as the first president of the United States, an executive office distinct from that, which was created only in 1789.

personas/elias-boudinot-nueva-jersey/res.texto: New Jersey lawyer, commissary of prisoners for Washington's army, and president of Congress from November 1782 to November 1783. During his term Congress ratified, on April 15, 1783, the preliminary articles of peace signed in Paris on November 30, 1782; in June 1783, in the face of the Pennsylvania mutiny, he moved Congress to Princeton. He was later a representative (1789-1795), director of the United States Mint until 1805, and first president of the American Bible Society. The young Cherokee Gallegina Uwatie (Buck Watie), the Elias Boudinot of the New Echota treaty, took his name.

personas/thomas-mifflin/resumen.texto: Philadelphia merchant, aide-de-camp to Washington, first Quartermaster General of the Continental Army, and major general. He presided over Congress from November 1783 to June 1784; at Annapolis he received Washington's resignation of his command on December 23, 1783, and Congress ratified the Treaty of Paris on January 14, 1784. He was the last president of Pennsylvania (1788-1790) and its first governor (1790-1799).

personas/benjamin-harrison-v/resumen.texto: Planter of Berkeley, in Charles City County, for decades a member of the House of Burgesses, delegate to the Continental Congress, where he chaired the Committee of the Whole for the final debate on the Declaration of Independence, and a signer of it. Governor of Virginia from late 1781, a month after Yorktown, until 1784, with a treasury emptied by the war and no resources to act beyond the immediate area; he preferred to deal with the Cherokees, Chickasaws, and Creeks rather than attack the peoples of the West, disagreeing with George Rogers Clark. In 1788 he voted against ratifying the Constitution because it did not include a bill of rights. He was the father of William Henry Harrison.

personas/thomas-nelson-jr/resumen.texto: Yorktown planter, delegate to the Continental Congress, signer of the Declaration of Independence, and brigadier general of the Virginia militia. The legislature elected him governor on June 12, 1781, after the nine days of William Fleming, and that year he fought in the siege of Yorktown, where according to tradition he offered five guineas to the first man who could hit his own house, occupied by Cornwallis. He died in 1789, with his lands damaged by the war and harassed by creditors.

personas/william-fleming-virginia/resume.texto: Scottish physician, colonel of militia on Virginia's southwestern frontier, senator, and member of the governor's council. In June 1781, with the British invasion, the legislature met in Staunton when Jefferson's term had expired, and Fleming, the senior council member present, acted as governor without formal office from June 4 to 12, until Nelson was elected. He called out the militia against the forces of Arnold and Tarleton, and the legislature later legalized his acts, which is why he appears as the third governor. He should not be confused with Judge William Fleming, a delegate to the Continental Congress.

personas/david-jameson-virginia/resumen.texto: Yorktown merchant and inventor, treasurer of the Society for Promoting Useful Knowledge (1773), senator of Virginia from 1776, and adviser to Patrick Henry. In 1781 he briefly served as acting governor during an illness of Thomas Nelson; the dates given for this vary between August and November of that year. He returned to the Senate in 1783.

personas/cornelis-jacobsen-mey/resumen.texto: Dutch captain and fur trader, perhaps from Hoorn, who between 1614 and 1621 sailed the Hudson River and Delaware Bay for the companies of New Netherland and built Fort Nassau on the Delaware. In 1624 he captained the Nieu Nederlandt, which brought the first families of settlers, mostly Walloons, to the Hudson and the Delaware, and he was the colony's first director, briefly, until Willem Verhulst succeeded him in 1625; during that time Fort Orange was completed. Cape May, in New Jersey, bears his name.

personas/philip-carteret-nueva-jersey/re.texto: Cousin of Sir George Carteret, one of the two proprietors of New Jersey, who in 1665 appointed him the first governor of the province, which had been taken from the Dutch in 1664. He chose Elizabethtown as capital, where the assembly met in 1668, and distributed land under the Concessions and Agreements, which guaranteed liberty of conscience. He governed until 1673 and again East Jersey from 1674; in 1680 Edmund Andros, governor of New York, had him arrested and taken to New York, where a jury acquitted him, and he died in December 1682.

personas/james-wilkinson/resumen.texto: Maryland officer, brigadier general of the United States Army, and its highest-ranking officer in two periods: after the death of Anthony Wayne, in December 1796, for a year and a half, until July 1798, and from June 15, 1800, to January 27, 1812. He took possession of Louisiana with Claiborne on December 20, 1803, and was the first governor of the Territory of Louisiana (1805-1807).
