It came after the loss of New York and a retreat through New Jersey, in which 90% of the soldiers who had fought at Long Island had left.

hechos/batallas-de-saratoga/resumen.texto: On 19 September and 7 October 1777 the Continental Army halted, at Saratoga, New York, the advance down the Hudson of General John Burgoyne, who had marched from Quebec. In the first battle, Freeman's Farm, Burgoyne held the field at a cost of about 600 casualties; in the second he was surrounded and on 17 October surrendered his entire army to Horatio Gates. Most of his Indigenous allies had abandoned him after the defeat at Bennington. News of the surrender was decisive for the Franco-American alliance of 1778.

hechos/batalla-de-oriskany/resumen.texto: On 6 August 1777 a column of Tryon County militia and Oneidas, under Nicholas Herkimer, marching to relieve Fort Stanwix, fell into an ambush by Mohawks, Senecas, Cayugas, Onondagas and Mississaugas, and by Loyalists, led by John Johnson. The Americans suffered about 465 killed, wounded or captured, nearly half the column; Herkimer, wounded, died on 16 August. Johnson's forces lost 93. It was the first time the Haudenosaunee fought one another: the Oneidas and Tuscaroras supported the patriots, while the Mohawks, Senecas, Cayugas and Onondagas supported the Crown.

hechos/batalla-de-wyoming/resumen.texto: On 3 July 1778, in the Wyoming Valley (Pennsylvania), Loyalist soldiers with Iroquois warriors defeated the patriot militia in half an hour, and the militia broke and scattered: about 300 were killed, many cut down while fleeing, and some of those captured were tortured and killed. Major John Butler reported that his allies took 227 scalps and five prisoners, and that no one was wounded who was not under arms; the writer Crèvecœur, who was in the valley weeks later, said the same. Colonel Zebulon Denison reported 302 dead. Buildings were looted and burned throughout the valley. Accounts of a massacre of hundreds of women and children, published weeks later in American newspapers, were not confirmed, and historians reject them; the accounts gave the battle the name “Wyoming massacre”.

hechos/teatro-occidental-de-la-independe.texto: The western front of the War of Independence
Ohio Country (representative point of the front, with estimated coordinates)

Combat zone west of the Appalachians, in the present-day Old Northwest and the states of Arkansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Missouri and Tennessee, where Indigenous peoples, with their British allies from Detroit, fought colonists to the south and east of the Ohio, and the Spanish fought as allies of the colonists. The treaties of Fort Stanwix and Hard Labour (1768) had opened lands south of the Ohio to colonists; Shawnees such as Blackfish and Mingos such as Pluggy attacked Kentucky to drive them out. George Rogers Clark took Kaskaskia on 4 July 1778 and subdued Vincennes; the Gnadenhutten massacre (1782) and the Battle of Blue Licks (1782) were among the last episodes.

hechos/sitio-de-pensacola/resumen.texto: From 9 March to 10 May 1781 Bernardo de Gálvez, with almost 8,000 men, besieged Pensacola, capital of British West Florida, and forced General John Campbell to surrender: more than 1,100 prisoners were taken; the British had about 200 casualties and the Spanish 74 killed and 198 wounded. Between 1,500 and 2,000 Indigenous people had come to Pensacola at various times to defend it on the British side. It concluded the Spanish conquest of West Florida in that war, and earned Gálvez the governorship of West Florida and of Louisiana.

hechos/sitio-de-yorktown/resumen.texto: In late September 1781 George Washington's army and Rochambeau's French troops, with the French fleet in the bay, besieged Cornwallis's army at Yorktown, Virginia, which surrendered on 19 October with more than 7,000 soldiers. It was the last major land battle of the war and led to the negotiations that ended in the Treaty of Paris of 1783; on the western frontier, where Indigenous peoples allied with the British kept fighting, combat continued until 1782.

hechos/batalla-de-blue-licks/resumen.texto: On 19 August 1782, ten months after Yorktown, some 50 of Butler's rangers and 300 Indigenous warriors (Shawnees, Mingos, Wyandots, Miamis, Ottawas, Ojibwes and Potawatomis) ambushed and defeated, by the Licking River, 182 Kentucky militiamen, among them Daniel Boone: 77 militiamen were killed and 6 captured, while among the attackers one ranger and 10 warriors were killed. Shortly afterwards more than a thousand Kentuckians destroyed five empty Shawnee villages on the Great Miami, in the last major offensive of the war.

hechos/batalla-de-los-arboles-caidos/res.texto: On 20 August 1794 the Legion of the United States of General Anthony Wayne, with Kentucky militiamen, defeated near the Maumee River, among trees felled by a tornado, a force of Shawnees under Blue Jacket, Ottawas under Egushawa and others of the Northwest Confederacy. Wayne had 33 killed and about 100 wounded and counted 30 to 40 warriors dead; the British official Alexander McKee reported 19. Fleeing warriors found the gates of the British Fort Miami closed, its commander unwilling to risk a war with the United States. It was the last battle of the Northwest War; the Treaty of Greenville (1795) ceded most of Ohio.

hechos/expedicion-de-lewis-y-clark/resum.texto: American military expedition ordered by Thomas Jefferson after the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. Led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, it left Camp Dubois on 14 May 1804, went up the Missouri, crossed the Continental Divide and reached the Pacific in 1805, where it wintered at Fort Clatsop; it returned on 23 September 1806. It passed through the lands of many Indigenous peoples: it wintered in 1804–1805 with the Mandan, where the hunter Toussaint Charbonneau joined with his Shoshone wife Sacagawea, and had a tense encounter with the Lakota near Fort Pierre. Only one member died, Sergeant Charles Floyd, on 20 August 1804. York, a slave belonging to Clark, also travelled with the expedition. The only deadly clash was in July 1806, on the Marias River, when Lewis's group killed two Blackfeet who were trying to take their guns and horses.

hechos/batalla-de-tippecanoe/resumen.texto: On 7 November 1811 the governor of the Indiana Territory, William Henry Harrison, who had marched his army to Prophetstown, was attacked before dawn, next to the village, by warriors of the confederation of Tecumseh, who was absent, under the command of his brother Tenskwatawa, the Prophet. The warriors numbered some 500, though estimates range from 350 to 1,000. The battle lasted about two hours; Harrison had 188 casualties, of whom 62 were killed or mortally wounded. Among the Indigenous fighters up to 50 were killed and 70 to 80 wounded. Harrison had the village cemetery dug up and burned the village.

hechos/terremotos-de-nuevo-madrid/resume.texto: A series of earthquakes began on 16 December 1811, with an estimated magnitude between 7.2 and 8.2, and continued with aftershocks of similar magnitude in January and February 1812: the strongest east of the Rockies in historical times. The epicenters lay between northeastern Arkansas and New Madrid, then in the Louisiana Territory (the one of 16 December 1811 was in northeastern Arkansas). The region had a small population, and how many died is unknown. Tecumseh's confederation read them as a sign that they had to support him and his brother the Prophet, and after the defeat at Tippecanoe the Indigenous people who followed them saw them as confirmation of their warnings.

hechos/guerra-de-1812/resumen.texto: The United States declared war on Great Britain on 18 June 1812 over British restrictions on trade and the forced recruitment of sailors from American ships; British support for the Indigenous confederations that resisted expansion in the Old Northwest also strained relations. Isaac Brock and Tecumseh took Detroit in 1812; Tecumseh died at the Battle of the Thames (1813). In the Southeast the Americans and their Indigenous allies defeated the Red Stick Creeks. The Treaty of Ghent (December 1814) restored the situation as it had been before the war; its Article 9 committed the United States to end hostilities with the Indigenous peoples and to restore to them their rights and possessions of 1811.

hechos/batalla-del-tamesis/resumen.texto: On 5 October 1813, near Moraviantown (Upper Canada), the mounted cavalry of General William Henry Harrison defeated the British division of Henry Procter, which had some 450 men present, and the Indigenous warriors who supported Tecumseh, who was killed in the fighting. Harrison reported 7 killed and 22 wounded; the British had between 12 and 18 killed and some 600 taken prisoner, and counted 16 Indigenous dead, while Harrison said he had found 33. Harrison afterwards burned Moraviantown, a village of Christian Lenape. The British lost control of western Ontario, and Tecumseh's confederation came apart. Harrison's horsemen shouted “Remember the Raisin!”, in reference to the American defeat at Frenchtown in January, where about 400 were killed and 547 captured: after the battle, Potawatomi warriors allied with Procter killed some 60 wounded prisoners.

hechos/guerra-creek/lugar.texto: Fort Mims (1813 attack, representative site of the Creek War)

hechos/guerra-creek/resumen.texto: Conflict among factions of the Muscogee (Creeks), European powers and the United States. The Red Sticks, the faction that resisted American expansion, attacked Fort Mims, north of Mobile, on 30 August 1813, where Creek mixed-blood people from the Tensaw settlement had taken refuge, and killed between 400 and 500 people, among them women and children. Militias from Tennessee, Georgia and the Mississippi Territory, with allied Lower Creeks, Cherokees and Choctaws, defeated them; at Tallushatchee (November 1813) John Coffee's cavalry killed many Red Sticks, among them women and children. In August 1814, by the Treaty of Fort Jackson, Andrew Jackson forced the Creek confederation to cede more than 21 million acres in southern Georgia and central Alabama, including lands of the Lower Creeks who had fought on Jackson's side, despite their protests.

hechos/batalla-de-horseshoe-bend/resumen.texto: On 27 March 1814 Andrew Jackson, with the 39th Infantry, Tennessee militia and some 600 Cherokees, Choctaws and Lower Creeks, attacked the fortified Red Stick camp on a bend of the Tallapoosa River and ended the Creek War. About 800 of the 1,000 warriors present were killed, two hundred of them shot by Coffee's troops as they tried to cross the river, as well as women and children from the camp. Jackson lost fewer than 50 men and had 154 wounded. His soldiers counted the dead by cutting off the tips of their noses, and made reins from the skin of some of them.

hechos/tratado-de-adams-onis/resumen.texto: Signed on 22 February 1819 by John Quincy Adams and Luis de Onís, by which Spain ceded East and West Florida to the United States, and the United States gave up its claims to Texas. It fixed the first transcontinental border, and Spain gave up its claims to the Oregon Country. The United States set up a commission for its citizens' claims against Spain, which distributed about 5 million dollars. Madrid delayed ratification until October 1820. The treaty was in full force until August 1821, when the Treaty of Córdoba recognized the independence of Mexico.

hechos/guerra-arikara/resumen.texto: On 2 June 1823 Arikara warriors attacked, on the Missouri, trappers of William Ashley's Rocky Mountain Fur Company and killed twenty men and wounded nine. The Arikara resented that Ashley had cut them out of their role as middlemen in the fur trade. Lieutenant Colonel Henry Leavenworth marched with 230 soldiers of the 6th Infantry, 750 Sioux (enemies of the Arikara) and 50 hunters and employees. He did not defeat them outright and signed a peace on 11 August. It was the first military conflict of the United States with Indigenous peoples west of the Missouri, and the Sioux continued to attack the Arikara.

hechos/guerra-winnebago/resumen.texto: A brief conflict of 1827 in the upper Mississippi, mainly in Wisconsin, limited to a few attacks by part of the Winnebago (Ho-Chunk) on American civilians. It was a reaction to the invasion of their lands by lead miners and to false rumors that two Ho-Chunk prisoners had been sent to a rival people to be executed. The chiefs handed over eight participants, among them Red Bird, whom the Americans believed to be the leader and who died in prison in 1828; two men convicted of homicide were pardoned by John Quincy Adams. The Ho-Chunk had to cede the lead region, and the United States built Fort Winnebago and reoccupied two other forts.

hechos/guerra-de-halcon-negro/resumen.texto: In April 1832 the Sauk leader Black Hawk crossed the Mississippi with Sauks, Meskwakis (Fox) and Kickapoos, the “British Band”, into Illinois, apparently to recover lands ceded by the disputed Treaty of St. Louis of 1804. The chiefs had no authorization from their councils to cede those lands and, according to the historian Patrick Jung, believed they were ceding less land than the text included. Militia fired on a delegation on 14 May; Black Hawk won at Stillman's Run, but his band, harried by hunger and desertion, was reduced. On 2 August the remnants of the British Band, some 500 people with about 150 warriors, were caught at Bad Axe while trying to cross the Mississippi. At least 260 died, about 110 of them drowned, and militiamen deliberately killed non-combatants; the historian Patrick Jung calls it “less a battle than a massacre”. The day before, Black Hawk had raised a white flag that the men of the steamboat Warrior did not accept, and he had moved north; he surrendered on 27 August. The Dakotas, who had offered the Americans 150 warriors, caught up with those who had crossed into Iowa and killed 68. Afterwards the tribes sold some 6 million acres of eastern Iowa for 20,000 dollars a year for 30 years.

hechos/guerras-seminolas/resumen.texto: Three wars between the United States and the Seminoles in Florida, between 1816 and 1858, which the Seminole people of Florida count as a single long war, since even between the fighting the violence of settlers, militias and slave catchers continued. The Seminoles formed in northern Florida in the eighteenth century and took in enslaved people fleeing from Georgia, which led to slave raids across the border. The first began with the destruction of Negro Fort in July 1816 (a shot from the American fleet blew up the fort's magazine, where Black maroons and Choctaws lived, and almost all its occupants died) and the invasion of Andrew Jackson (1817–1818), which razed Seminole, Miccosukee and Black Seminole villages and took St. Marks and, briefly, Pensacola. Spain ceded Florida by the Adams-Onís Treaty, and the Seminoles were moved to the center of the peninsula by the Treaty of Moultrie Creek. The second war ran from 1835 to 1842 and the third from 1855 to 1858.

hechos/segunda-guerra-seminola/resumen.texto: War of the United States against the Seminoles, among them Creeks and Black Seminoles, in Florida, after the Treaty of Payne's Landing (1832), which provided for their removal, and the Indian Removal Act of 1830. It began on 28 December 1835, when Seminoles ambushed a column of 110 men leaving Fort Brooke under Major Dade and killed all but three. In 1837 General Thomas Jesup seized Osceola and Coacoochee when they came to parley under a white flag. It lasted more than six years, mostly in small engagements: the Seminoles began with between 900 and 1,400 warriors and had no way to replace their losses. The army declared the end on 14 August 1842 without a peace treaty, with only a few hundred Seminoles left in Florida; by 1842 some 3,600 had been removed to Indian Territory.

hechos/guerras-indias-de-texas/resumen.texto: A series of conflicts between the settlers of Texas and the Indigenous peoples of the southern plains during the nineteenth century. Spain and then Mexico had encouraged the colonization of Texas to have a buffer zone against those peoples. The clashes continued after Texan independence (1836) and did not end until 1875, when the Quahadi Comanches of Quanah Parker, the last free band, surrendered and moved to the Fort Sill reservation. There were massacres on both sides: the Comanche raids reached deep into the interior of Mexico and carried off captives, and the Texan president Mirabeau Lamar proclaimed in 1839 a war to drive out the Indigenous peoples, which began with the expulsion of the Cherokees from Texas (about 100 died, among them the chief Bowles).

hechos/gran-incursion-comanche-de-1840/r.texto: Comanche raid of August 1840 on towns of the Republic of Texas, which followed the fight at the Council House (San Antonio, 19 March 1840). There Republic officials tried to take 33 Comanche chiefs and their wives as prisoners, in exchange for the thirteen captives they were expected to hand over. The delegation brought only one, Matilda Lockhart, because the Comanches demanded a ransom for each one. According to the report of Colonel Hugh McLeod, 35 Comanches (30 men, 3 women and 2 children) and 7 Texans died at the Council House; the Comanches afterwards tortured and killed 13 captives. The Penateka Comanches led by Buffalo Hump plundered Linnville, the second port of the Republic, on 8 August, with goods valued at more than 300,000 dollars; in the raid they killed some 23 unarmed civilians in the Victoria and Linnville area. They were caught on 12 August at Plum Creek by militia and rangers, where they killed captives such as Mrs. Crosby.

hechos/guerra-anglo-cheroqui/resumen.texto: The Cherokees, allies of the British when the French and Indian War began, clashed with them in 1758 over colonial pressure, and because Virginians killed and scalped between 30 and 40 Cherokee warriors who had taken horses they believed were theirs, and afterwards collected the bounty by saying they were Shawnee scalps. Thirty-eight chiefs were taken as hostages at Fort Prince George. When the Cherokees attacked the fort to free them, in February 1760, the garrison killed 16 hostages, and the Cherokees besieged Fort Loudoun, which surrendered in August 1760. The day after the garrison left, some 700 Cherokees attacked the column at Cane Creek, killed 29 (among them the commander, Paul Demeré, and three women) and took almost all the rest prisoner. In 1761 James Grant entered Cherokee country with 2,800 men, defeated the Cherokees at Echoee Pass and razed some 18 villages of the Middle Towns; some towns were never reoccupied. The war ended in November 1761 with the Treaty of Long Island of Holston with Virginia.

hechos/tratado-de-san-lorenzo-1795/titul.texto: The Treaty of San Lorenzo (Pinckney Treaty)

hechos/tratado-de-san-lorenzo-1795/resum.texto: Signed on 27 October 1795 by Thomas Pinckney and Manuel Godoy, it fixed the border between the United States and Spanish Florida and guaranteed Americans the right to navigate the Mississippi. Its Article V obliges each country to contain by force any hostility from the Indigenous peoples living within its limits, and not to make alliance treaties with those on the other side, except treaties of peace; it provides that trade with them shall be common. Until then Spain had supplied them with weapons for years. The treaty left within the limits of the United States the lands of the Chickasaws and Choctaws, who did not take part. The Senate gave its consent on 5 March 1796, and the United States ratified it on the 7th.

hechos/fraude-de-las-tierras-de-yazoo/lu.texto: Yazoo River (lands sold, in present-day Mississippi and Alabama)

hechos/fraude-de-las-tierras-de-yazoo/re.texto: In 1794 speculating companies were formed, and the Georgia legislature, by a law (the Yazoo Act) that Governor George Mathews signed on 7 January 1795, sold to them at very low prices large expanses of the Yazoo lands, in what are today parts of Alabama and Mississippi, which were claimed and occupied by Indigenous peoples and in part also claimed by Spain. The law was annulled on 13 February 1796, but in Fletcher v. Peck (1810) the Supreme Court ruled that the contracts were binding and that the state could not annul them retroactively; in 1802 Georgia ceded its claims to the federal government. The Choctaw and Chickasaw claims had not been extinguished; they were extinguished through a series of treaties, the last of them the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830, Choctaws) and the Treaty of Pontotoc Creek (1832, Chickasaws).

hechos/guerras-chickasaw/lugar.texto: Tupelo (area of the battles of Ogoula Tchetoka and Ackia, 1736)

hechos/guerras-chickasaw/resumen.texto: Wars of the first half of the eighteenth century between the Chickasaws, allies of the British, and the French with their Choctaw, Quapaw and Illinois Confederation allies, for control of the communications of Louisiana along the Mississippi. In 1721 Bienville incited the Choctaws to attack Chickasaw villages. On 25 March 1736 the French and the Illinois were defeated at Ogoula Tchetoka, and on 26 May Bienville, with 1,200 French and Choctaws, was repulsed at Ackia, near Tupelo. The French never defeated the Chickasaws, who defended their territory at great cost in population and in their way of life; the wars ended with the cession of New France to Great Britain in 1763.

hechos/guerras-navajo/resumen.texto: Three periods of conflict of the Navajo (Diné) with the Spanish until 1821, with Mexico until 1848 and with the United States afterwards, ranging from small raids to large government expeditions, together with a cycle of mutual raids with other peoples and with settlers: New Mexicans captured Navajos to sell as slaves, and the Navajos carried off livestock and captives. In 1641–1642 the Franciscans organized a campaign against the Navajos that burned their cornfields. Facundo Melgares, the last Spanish governor of New Mexico, made two unsuccessful expeditions and asked for peace in October 1821. In 1863 General James Carleton ordered 18 Navajo chiefs to surrender before 20 July 1863 and move to Bosque Redondo, while Kit Carson conducted a simultaneous campaign that burned crops and homes. The treaty of June 1868 allowed their return.

hechos/primera-expedicion-a-kamchatka/re.texto: Commissioned by Peter the Great in 1724 and led by Vitus Bering, it was Russia's first scientific naval expedition. It spent two years travelling from St. Petersburg to Okhotsk, and in July and August 1728 sailed along the Pacific coast as far as St. Lawrence Island, passed through the Bering Strait and reached the Chukchi Sea, without sighting the North American coast. It returned believing it had accomplished its task, and reached St. Petersburg on 28 February 1730. It produced evidence that Asia and America are not joined, and was followed by the Second Kamchatka Expedition (1732).

hechos/revuelta-de-boston-1689/resumen.texto: On 18 April 1689 militiamen and residents of Boston arrested the governor of the Dominion of New England, Edmund Andros, and Dominion officials, with no casualties on either side. Andros had made enemies among the colonists by enforcing the Navigation Acts, denying the validity of existing land titles, restricting town assemblies and promoting the Church of England. The revolt occurred when James II had been deposed in England. The leaders of the former Massachusetts Bay Colony regained government, and in other colonies those displaced by the Dominion returned to power.

hechos/expedicion-de-chamuscado-y-rodrig.texto: Expedition that Friar Agustín Rodríguez organized from Santa Barbara and that Captain Francisco Sánchez, “El Chamuscado,” led. It left on June 5, 1581, with nine soldiers, three friars, and Indigenous servants; it descended the Conchos River to the Rio Grande and followed that river to the Pueblo villages of New Mexico. They were the first Spaniards to visit the Pueblo peoples since Coronado, some forty years earlier.

hechos/expedicion-de-espejo/resumen.texto: Antonio de Espejo, a wealthy rancher accused of homicide who had taken refuge in Santa Barbara, financed an expedition that set out on November 10, 1582, with fourteen soldiers and a priest, ostensibly to learn what had become of two friars who had stayed among the pueblos. He followed Chamuscado's route and reached New Mexico and Arizona; his journey stirred interest in founding a Spanish colony among the Rio Grande pueblos.

hechos/camino-real-de-tierra-adentro/tit.texto: El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro

hechos/camino-real-de-tierra-adentro/res.texto: Spanish road of 2560 km between Mexico City and San Juan Pueblo (Ohkay Owingeh), in New Mexico, used from 1598 to 1882 and also known as the Silver Route. It crossed northern Mexico and linked the mines and towns along the way with the province of New Mexico. After the revolt of 1680, the conducta caravans supplied the missions, presidios, and ranches of the north along it.

hechos/fundacion-de-el-paso-del-norte/ti.texto: Founding of El Paso del Norte

hechos/fundacion-de-el-paso-del-norte/re.texto: On December 8, 1659, the Franciscan friar García de San Francisco founded the Mission of Our Lady of Guadalupe of the Mansos of the Paso del Río del Norte, origin of Ciudad Juárez, at the crossing where the Camino Real passed. It was then the second center of evangelization in New Mexico, after Santa Fe. El Paso (Texas), which later grew on the north bank, inherited its name.

hechos/don-luis-llevado-a-espana/resumen.texto: In June 1561 the caravel Santa Catalina, sent by the viceroy Luis de Velasco, entered Chesapeake Bay, and its captain, Antonio Velázquez, took two Indigenous people as interpreters, one of them Paquiquineo. He reached Seville that year and Mexico City in 1562, where he was baptized as Luis de Velasco. In 1570 he returned as a guide for the Jesuits of the Ajacán mission, and it is believed he took part in its massacre; some historians believe he was the future Opechancanough, a claim others deny.

hechos/capitulacion-de-quebec-1759/resum.texto: On September 18, 1759, five days after the battle on the Plains of Abraham, the king's lieutenant Jean-Baptiste Nicolas Roch de Ramezay surrendered Quebec to Admiral Charles Saunders and General George Townshend. The British granted the eleven conditions he requested: the honors of war, the protection of civilians and their property, and the free exercise of the Catholic religion. In April 1760 Lévis won at Sainte-Foy but could not retake the city, lacking naval support.

hechos/capitulacion-de-montreal-1760/res.texto: On September 8, 1760, after two months of campaigning, the governor general of New France, the Marquis de Vaudreuil, signed with General Jeffery Amherst, in the British camp before Montreal, 55 articles that handed Canada over to Great Britain. Vaudreuil asked that the French, Canadians, Acadians, and Indigenous peoples have the rights of the other British subjects. Amherst granted most of it (free Catholic worship, the property of the inhabitants and of the seigneurs, amnesty for the Canadian militiamen, and possession of Black and Indigenous enslaved people), but he denied the honors of war to the French troops, who could not serve again in that war; rejected that the King of France name the bishop and that the Jesuits, Recollets, and Sulpicians remain; and on the Acadians answered that they were already British subjects. Article 40 recognized the lands and religion of the Indigenous allies, although they had not taken part in drafting it. With it, the major operations in North America came to an end.

hechos/expedicion-de-braddock/resumen.texto: British campaign of 1755 to take Fort Duquesne, at the forks of the Ohio, under General Edward Braddock, commander in chief in America. It left Fort Cumberland, Maryland, on May 29 with some 2100 men, among them the 44th and 48th regiments and provincial troops, and opened a road of about 180 km across the Allegheny Mountains, at times covering just 3 km a day. Braddock obtained only eight Mingo scouts and advanced with a light column of some 1300 men, leaving the baggage to Thomas Dunbar. Franklin helped gather wagons, whose teamsters included Daniel Boone and Daniel Morgan, and Washington accompanied him as a volunteer aide. After the defeat on July 9 at the Monongahela, Braddock died on the 13th during the retreat, and Dunbar burned some 150 wagons and destroyed cannon and provisions before turning back; Fort Duquesne remained French until 1758.

hechos/accion-del-8-de-junio-de-1755/res.texto: With France and Britain still at peace, three British ships of Vice Admiral Edward Boscawen's squadron, the Dunkirk, the Defiance, and the Torbay, caught off Newfoundland, south of Cape Race, three ships of Dubois de la Motte's French fleet that were carrying troops to Canada. According to the most repeated account, Hocquart, of the Alcide, asked Richard Howe, of the Dunkirk, whether they were at war or at peace, and Howe answered “peace, peace” just before opening fire at pistol range. The Alcide, a 64-gun ship, held out for five hours and surrendered together with the Lys, which carried eight companies of the Queen's and Languedoc regiments; the Dauphin Royal escaped in the fog. The two countries formally declared war on each other in the spring of 1756.

hechos/batalla-de-sabbath-day-point/titu.texto: The Battle of Sabbath Day Point

hechos/batalla-de-sabbath-day-point/resu.texto: On July 23, 1757, on Lake George, some 450 French and Indigenous fighters under Ensign de Corbière ambushed some 350 militiamen of the Jersey Blues of Colonel John Parker, whom Monro had sent in boats to reconnoiter from Fort William Henry. The French had captured three advance boats earlier, and the prisoners, questioned by the Indigenous warriors, revealed where Parker was going to land. About 160 were killed or drowned, and the rest were taken prisoner or escaped, some 100 with Parker; the French reported only one man slightly wounded. Two weeks later the French were before Fort William Henry.

hechos/batalla-de-las-raquetas-de-nieve/.texto: On January 21, 1757, near Fort Carillon, a column of Rogers' Rangers (86 men when they left Fort William Henry), returning by the same road after capturing seven prisoners, fell into an ambush by some 90 regulars of the Languedoc regiment, under Captain de Basserode, and as many Canadian militiamen and Indigenous warriors, chiefly Ottawas led by Charles Michel de Langlade, according to the report of Lusignan, commander of Carillon; Rogers estimated them at 250. Many French muskets misfired because of wet powder, and John Stark held a line on a rise; the fighting ended at nightfall with heavy losses on both sides. Rogers, twice wounded, ordered the prisoners killed so that he could move faster, and he reached Fort William Henry on the 23rd with 48 healthy men and six wounded. The French said the snowshoes gave the English an advantage.

hechos/sitio-de-fort-niagara-1759/resume.texto: From July 6 to 26, 1759, a British army of some 3200 regulars and provincials under John Prideaux, with several hundred Haudenosaunee led by William Johnson, besieged the French fort of Captain Pierre Pouchot, as part of the campaign to take the Great Lakes and the Ohio Valley from France. Prideaux died on the 20th when one of his own artillery shells burst, and Johnson took command, although he was a provincial officer and disputed his right to it with Lieutenant Colonel Frederick Haldimand. After the French relief force was defeated on the 24th at La Belle-Famille, Pouchot capitulated on the 26th. The French then burned Fort Rouillé (Toronto), and in August they abandoned and burned the Ohio forts, such as Machault.

hechos/batalla-de-la-belle-famille/resum.texto: On July 24, 1759, about three kilometers south of Fort Niagara, the relief force of François-Marie Le Marchand de Lignery and Charles Philippe Aubry, assembled at Fort Machault with allied Indigenous warriors, fell into an ambush by Lieutenant Colonel Eyre Massey, who had 464 regulars and had entrenched the road. The Indigenous allies of the British had warned those allied with the French that they would remain neutral, and many of the latter left. The British rose up and fired at close range, charged with the bayonet, and the Haudenosaunee pursued those who fled. Lignery was mortally wounded, and Michel Maray de La Chauvignerie was taken prisoner. Pouchot capitulated two days later.

lugares/san-agustin-florida/resumen.texto: Founded by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés in 1565 next to the Timucua village of Seloy, it was the capital of Spanish Florida and the base of its missions. It is the oldest city of European origin inhabited without interruption in the continental territory of the United States.

lugares/santa-fe-nuevo-mexico/resumen.texto: Villa founded around 1610 as the capital of New Mexico, besieged and taken by the Pueblo peoples in the 1680 revolt and recovered by Diego de Vargas in 1693. It is the oldest state capital in the United States.

lugares/quebec/resumen.texto: Founded by Champlain in 1608 on the site of the Iroquoian village of Stadacona, it was the capital of New France and the seat of its bishopric, seminary, hospital and Ursuline convent. It passed to Great Britain after the battle of 1759.

lugares/montreal/resumen.texto: Founded in 1642 as Ville-Marie, a mission of French devotees, on the island where Cartier had visited the Iroquoian village of Hochelaga in 1535. It was the center of New France’s fur trade and the site of the Great Peace of 1701.

lugares/jamestown/resumen.texto: The first permanent English settlement in America, founded in 1607 on land of the Powhatan Confederacy, and capital of Virginia until 1699. Excavations since 1994 found the original fort, which was thought to have been lost in the river.

lugares/filadelfia/resumen.texto: City founded by William Penn in 1682 on land bought from the Lenape. It was the largest city of the Thirteen Colonies and the seat of the Continental Congresses, of the Declaration of Independence and of the 1787 constitutional convention.

lugares/nueva-york/resumen.texto: Founded as New Amsterdam by the Dutch West India Company on the island of Manhattan, on Lenape territory, it was the capital of New Netherland until the English took it in 1664 and renamed it.

lugares/boston/resumen.texto: Founded in 1630 by the Puritans of the Massachusetts Bay Company on the Shawmut peninsula, it was the political and religious center of New England.

lugares/plymouth-massachusetts/resumen.texto: Founded in 1620 by the passengers of the Mayflower on the abandoned village of Patuxet, whose inhabitants had died in the 1616–1619 epidemic. It was the capital of the Plymouth Colony until 1691.

lugares/nueva-orleans/resumen.texto: Founded by Bienville in 1718 near the mouth of the Mississippi, it was the capital of French Louisiana and, from 1763 to 1800, of Spanish Louisiana. The United States bought it with Louisiana in 1803.

lugares/natick/resumen.texto: The first “praying town” of Christian Indians, founded by John Eliot in 1651 on the banks of the Charles River, with its own government and school. After King Philip’s War it lost population, and its lands gradually passed into the hands of colonists.

lugares/novoarkhangelsk/resumen.texto: Founded by Baranov in 1804 next to the Tlingit fort captured that year, it was the capital of Russian America until 1867; the transfer of Alaska to the United States took place there.

lugares/castillo-de-san-marcos/resumen.texto: Coquina stone fortress built between 1672 and 1695 to defend St. Augustine, partly with the labor of Indians from the missions. It withstood English sieges in 1702 and 1740.

lugares/fuerte-carolina/resumen.texto: Fort of the French Huguenots next to the San Juan River, in Timucua land, taken by Menéndez de Avilés in September 1565. Its exact location has not been found.

lugares/fuerte-mose/nombre.texto: Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose

lugares/fuerte-mose/resumen.texto: Fortified town of Africans who had fled Carolina and gained their freedom in Spanish Florida, north of St. Augustine. Its inhabitants left for Cuba in 1763 when Florida passed to Great Britain.

lugares/mision-san-luis-de-apalache/resu.texto: Capital of the province of Apalachee, with a mission, a fort and the council house of the Apalachee chief, today reconstructed in Tallahassee on the basis of excavations. It was abandoned in 1704 in the face of attacks from Carolina.

lugares/palacio-de-los-gobernadores/nomb.texto: Palace of the Governors of Santa Fe

lugares/palacio-de-los-gobernadores/resu.texto: Seat of the government of New Mexico since around 1610, occupied by Pueblo peoples after the 1680 revolt and recovered in 1693. It is one of the oldest public buildings in the United States.

lugares/hawikuh/resumen.texto: Zuni pueblo where Estebanico died in 1539 and which Coronado took by assault in July 1540, believing it was Cíbola. It had a Franciscan mission from 1629 and was abandoned at the time of the 1680 revolt.

lugares/mision-de-san-antonio-de-valero/.texto: Mission San Antonio de Valero (The Alamo)
Franciscan mission founded in 1718 for Coahuiltecan peoples, origin of San Antonio. Secularized in 1793, its church became the Alamo fort in the Texas War of 1836.

lugares/mision-de-san-saba/nombre.texto: Mission Santa Cruz de San Sabá

lugares/mision-de-san-saba/resumen.texto: Mission for the Lipan Apaches in central Texas, destroyed in March 1758 by Comanches and Wichitas.

lugares/mision-san-diego/resumen.texto: First mission in Alta California, founded by Junípero Serra in July 1769 on Kumeyaay land. It was burned by the Kumeyaay in November 1775 and rebuilt.

lugares/mision-san-carlos/nombre.texto: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

lugares/mision-san-carlos/resumen.texto: Founded in Monterey in 1770 and moved to Carmel in 1771, it was the seat of the president of the California missions; Junípero Serra is buried there.

lugares/mision-san-gabriel/resumen.texto: Mission founded in 1771 on Tongva land, near present-day Los Angeles, and the scene of Toypurina’s attempted rebellion in 1785.

lugares/fort-ross/resumen.texto: Post of the Russian-American Company on the California coast, founded in 1812 on Kashaya Pomo land to supply wheat to Alaska and to hunt sea otters with Alutiiq hunters. It was sold in 1841.

lugares/bahia-de-tres-santos/resumen.texto: First permanent Russian settlement in America, founded by Shelikhov in 1784 on Kodiak Island; in 1792 the seat was moved to present-day Kodiak city.

lugares/fort-pitt/resumen.texto: British fort built at the confluence that forms the Ohio River, on the site of the French Fort Duquesne. It was besieged in 1763 during Pontiac’s Rebellion; it is the origin of Pittsburgh.

lugares/werowocomoco/resumen.texto: Capital of Powhatan on the York River, where John Smith was taken in 1607–1608. Identified and excavated since 2003, it shows occupation from around the 13th century and trenches that delimited a central enclosure.

lugares/sainte-marie-entre-los-hurones/r.texto: Fortified base of the Jesuit mission in Huronia, with a chapel, hospital and workshops, which the Jesuits burned in 1649 when they fled Iroquois attacks. It was rebuilt in the 20th century based on the excavations.

lugares/hotel-dieu-de-quebec/resumen.texto: Hospital founded in 1639 by the Augustinian Hospitallers of Dieppe with funds from the Duchess of Aiguillon; it first cared for Indigenous people and is the oldest hospital in operation in Canada.

lugares/monasterio-de-las-ursulinas-de-q.texto: Convent and girls’ school founded in 1639 by Marie de l’Incarnation, the first girls’ school in New France, which admitted French and Indigenous students.

lugares/seminario-de-quebec/resumen.texto: Seminary founded by Bishop Laval in 1663 to train the clergy of New France; Laval University was born from it in 1852.

lugares/universidad-de-harvard/resumen.texto: College founded by the Massachusetts assembly in 1636 to train ministers, the oldest institution of higher education in the United States. Its 1650 charter included the education of youth “English and Indian.”

lugares/colegio-de-william-and-mary/resu.texto: Royal college founded in Williamsburg, Virginia, in 1693, which from 1723 had a school for Indigenous children in the Brafferton building.

lugares/dartmouth-college/resumen.texto: College founded in Hanover, New Hampshire, by Eleazar Wheelock in 1769, with a charter that destined it for Indigenous and English youth, financed with what Samson Occom raised in Great Britain.
